plants.name: Achacha
plants.origin: Amazon Basin, Bolivia (South America)
plants.economicUse: Fresh fruits are economical/commercial, orange-coloured, egg-shaped with sweet-tart flavour. Used in making fresh juice, jams, jellies & desserts. Recently commercialized in Australia.
plants.medicalSignificance: Traditionally known in Bolivian folk medicine for digestive issues, anti-inflammatory effects, and appetite suppression. It contains hydroxycitric acid (HCA), similar to Garcinia cambogia, though at lower concentrations. Marketed in some supplements for weight management.

plants.name: Grumichama
plants.vernacularName: Grumichama Cherry / Brazilian Cherry / Spanish Cherry / Grumixama
plants.origin: Atlantic Rainforests (Brazil)
plants.economicUse: Fresh fruits are eaten fresh and used in making jams, jellies, wine, and beverages. Attractive flowers and plants are used in subtropical landscaping.
plants.medicalSignificance: Potential application in nutraceuticals and functional medicine/foods. Rich in vitamin C, anthocyanins (purple pigments), polyphenols, and antioxidants. Has antimicrobial properties. Used in treating diarrhea and gastrointestinal discomfort.

plants.name: Savannah Cherry
plants.origin: Tropical Savanna, Brazilian Cerrado Biome
plants.economicUse: Small red fruits are sweet–sour, juicy, high in vitamin C & antioxidants. Eaten fresh and used in jams, jellies, and juices. It is a flavoring, coloring agent, and natural antioxidant for beverages and desserts.
plants.medicalSignificance: Used in Brazilian folk medicine. Potential superfruit due to high phenolic, flavonoid, and vitamin content. Rich in antioxidants, antibacterial, antifungal, anti-inflammatory, hypoglycemic and anti-diabetic.

plants.name: Jaboticaba
plants.origin: Brazil particularly Sao Paulo, Argentina
plants.economicUse: Fruits are used in jams, jellies, liquers, preserves and beverages.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in Vit C, anthocyanins, anti-oxidants, antimicrobials, anti-inflammatory. Treats diarrhea, asthma, tonsillitis, blood sugar control.

plants.name: Surinam Cherry
plants.origin: Brazil particularly Uruguay, Paraguay, Northern Argentina
plants.economicUse: Fresh fruits are bright red or dark purple ribbed berries used in flavouring sweet/tangy or slightly resinous foods. Used in making jams, jellies, liqueurs, beverages. Used in making ornamental bonsai. Fresh leaves are used in making herbal teas and mosquito repellent.
plants.medicalSignificance: Extracts are anti-malarial, anti-bacterial, anti-fungal, anti-inflammatory, blood sugar regulation, anti-obesity. Has cardiovascular effects.

plants.name: Lilly Pilly Pink
plants.origin: Australia, Eastern coastal rainforests of Queensland
plants.economicUse: Fruits are sweet to tart. Used in jams, jellies, sauces, syrups, cordial, desserts. In urban landscaping used as hedge plant or agro-forestry.
plants.medicalSignificance: Traditionally used by Aboriginal Australians as medicines for coughs, diarrhea and general digestive health. Is anti-oxidative and anti-inflammatory. Rich in flavonoids, anthocyanin, Vit-C. Treats blood sugar, skin health, immune regulation.

plants.name: Beauty Berry
plants.origin: Southeastern USA especially Texas, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia
plants.economicUse: Small, metallic purple berries are mildly sweet and have astringent properties. Used in making jams, jellies, wines, herbal teas. Used in landscaping and ornamental gardens.
plants.medicalSignificance: Roots used in treating dysentery, urinary tract issue, malarial repellent, rheumatism. Compounds like callicarpenal and intermedeol have insect-repelling activity. Leaves are anti-oxidative and anti-inflammatory.

plants.name: Mangosteen
plants.origin: Malay Peninsula, including Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, and the Philippines
plants.economicUse: Fruits are called 'Queen of fruits', fruit has white, juicy aromatic pulp. Fruits are used in making juices, jams, jellies, canned products, desserts and functional beverages. Fruit pulp is used in making nutraceuticals.
plants.medicalSignificance: Mangosteen (Vrishatphal) is mentioned in some regional and Siddha texts for treating diarrhea, skin eruptions, and inflammation. Mangosteen is classified as Kasjaya (astringent) and Tikta (bitter) in taste.

plants.name: Yellow Che Fruit
plants.origin: China, Japan & Korea
plants.economicUse: Mulberry-like fruits are mildly sweet in taste used for making jams, jellies, beverages, wines, juices.
plants.medicalSignificance: The fruits are antioxidant, liver tonic, anti-inflammatory, anticancerous, antidiabetic. Liver protective properties.

plants.name: Mamey Sapote
plants.origin: Central America & Mexico - Guatemala, Honduras, Northern South America
plants.economicUse: Fruits are known for excellent flavor, texture. Eaten fresh as smoothies, ice-creams, desserts, milkshakes and baby food. Suitable for home gardens, orchards, and agroforestry systems.
plants.medicalSignificance: Central American and Caribbean folk medicine for stomach pain, digestive disorder or liver tonic. Seeds used topically as a skin treatment.

plants.name: Australian Finger Lime
plants.origin: Eastern Australia (rainforests of Queensland and New South Wales)
plants.economicUse: Cultivated for its unique caviar-like pulp, eaten fresh and used for jams, jellies, beverages, sauces, and desserts.
plants.medicalSignificance: Finger lime has been traditionally used by Aboriginal Australians. It is used as a bush medicine for treating skin irritations and infection. High in antioxidants and Vit-C. Has antimicrobial properties, can be used in skin care products and nutraceuticals.

plants.name: Climber Mango
plants.origin: Indo-Myanmar region, Southeast Asia & Northeastern India
plants.economicUse: Economically used as a rootstock for grafting cultivated mango varieties. A great agroforestry specie with food crops.
plants.medicalSignificance: It is believed to be a folk medicine, helps with diarrhea, dysentery, and wound healing. It contains polyphenol and antioxidants.

plants.name: Lemba
plants.origin: Southeast Asia and the Indian subcontinent. Commonly in India, Sri Lanka, Indonesia
plants.economicUse: Economically used as ornamental plant due to its attractive flowers. Rhizomes are used in traditional medicines, cosmetics, shampoo and starch production.
plants.vedicSignificance: Mentioned in Ayurveda, Siddha, and Unani systems
plants.medicalSignificance: Rhizomes are used for antidiabetic (reduces blood sugar), antipyretic (fever reduction). It has anti-inflammatory, anti-oxidative, and anti-microbial properties. Used for treating skin diseases, bronchitis, intestinal worms, and urinary disorders.

plants.name: Date Palm Hybrid
plants.origin: Middle East and North Africa
plants.economicUse: It is grown for edible fruits rich in natural sugars, fiber, and minerals. Used for fresh consumption, dry fruits, and sweets. Used as agroforestry and horticulture development. It is popular in export and local markets—especially valuable in arid and semi-arid zones.
plants.medicalSignificance: Dates are widely used in Ayurveda as body tonics and aphrodisiacs. It is a digestive aid, mild laxative, and blood purifier. It is rich in iron, potassium, and antioxidants. It is helpful in anemia, fatigue, reproductive health, and heart health.

plants.name: Cedar Bay Cherry
plants.origin: Northern Australia (especially around Cedar Bay, Queensland), New Guinea, and nearby islands
plants.economicUse: It is grown for its sweet, cherry-like fruits. It is used in fresh consumption, jams, jellies and dessert.
plants.medicalSignificance: Traditionally used by Aboriginal Australians. Fruit consumed for general nourishment, leaves and bark sometimes used in folk remedies. Fruit is rich in antioxidants, Vit-C, and fiber. Potential anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial properties.

plants.name: Pineapple Medura
plants.origin: South America (particularly Brazil and Paraguay)
plants.economicUse: It is grown for sweet edible, juicy fruit. Used for juices, jams, canned products, desserts, confectionery and food processing industries. It is an important horticultural crop in tropical and subtropical regions.
plants.medicalSignificance: Mentioned in Ayurveda for aiding digestion (rich in bromelain, a digestive enzyme), treating inflammation, indigestion and intestinal worms. Other properties are anti-oxidants, anti-inflammatory and immune boosting. Juice is often used to treat sore throat and digestive sluggishness.

plants.name: Barbados Acerola Cherry
plants.vernacularName: Barbados Acerola Cherry / West Indian Cherry
plants.origin: Tropical Americas – especially the Caribbean, Central America, and northern South America
plants.economicUse: Barbados cherry is grown primarily for its extremely high Vit-C content. Used in making jams, jellies, supplements, powders and health drinks. It is used in cosmetic products. Medically, used in nutraceuticals and fortified foods.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in antioxidants, polyphenols, carotenoids. It is used for boosting immunity, skin health/skin rejuvenation, anti-aging and wound healing. It is helpful in combating scurvy, fatigue and common colds.

plants.name: Burmese Grape
plants.origin: Indo-Myanmar region, Southeast Asia & Northeastern India; especially Myanmar, NE India, Thailand, Bangladesh, Malaysia
plants.economicUse: Burmese grape is grown for its edible fruits, sweet to slightly sour in taste. It is consumed fresh, or used in juices, jams, and pickles. Also cultivated as a shade and ornamental tree for cultivating gardens/orchards.
plants.medicalSignificance: Traditionally used in folk and tribal medicine (especially in India and Southeast Asia). Fruits aid in digestion, act as a coolant. Bark and leaves are used for treating skin ailments, diarrhea, and infections. Rich in Vitamin C, iron, and antioxidants.

plants.name: Chamaliang
plants.origin: Native to Southeast Asia, particularly Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and northeastern India
plants.economicUse: Chamaliang is grown for its small, mango-like fruits. Fruits are eaten fresh, used in pickles, preserves, and desserts. Occasionally cultivated as an ornamental and fruit-bearing tree.
plants.medicalSignificance: Traditional uses in Southeast Asian folk medicine. Fruits are used for digestive aid. Leaves and bark are used to treat fever, skin infections, and cough. Rich in Vitamin C, carotenoids, and polyphenols.

plants.name: Tropical Rainforest Plum
plants.vernacularName: Tropical Rainforest Plum var. Merry Poza
plants.origin: Tropical regions of Southeast Asia, India, and Africa
plants.economicUse: Rainforest Plum is grown for edible fruits (small, tangy, plum-like). Used in jams, pickles, chutneys, and local beverages. Also planted as ornamental shrub/tree. It is used to make live fences or hedges (due to thorns).
plants.medicalSignificance: Traditionally used in folk and traditional medicine. Fruit treats digestive issues, diarrhea, and respiratory ailments. Leaves/Bark are antibacterial, antioxidant, and anti-inflammatory. Used for treating skin diseases, fever and wound healing.

plants.name: Water Apple
plants.origin: Southeast Asia – likely Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Andaman-Nicobar region
plants.economicUse: Fresh consumption: consumed raw for its crisp, watery texture. Used in making pickles, jams, jellies, preserves, juice and beverages. Also grown as an ornamental plant due to glossy leaves and attractive fruit. Used in agroforestry and landscaping.
plants.medicalSignificance: Believed to be cooling in nature and used for balancing Pitta and Kapha doshas in traditional Indian medicine. It is diuretic, aids hydration due to high water content, mildly laxative, anti-diabetic, anti-inflammatory, and leaves/bark are used for skin irritations.

plants.name: Mexican Sapote Black
plants.vernacularName: Mexican Sapote Black / Chocolate Pudding Fruit
plants.origin: Mexico, Central America, native to Southern Mexico, Guatemala & Colombia
plants.economicUse: Fruit is edible, ripe pulp resembles chocolate pudding in color and texture. Fruit is eaten fresh or used in smoothies, desserts, and baking. It is a natural sweetener, used in low-calorie dessert recipes.
plants.medicalSignificance: Fruit is rich in Vitamin-C and Vitamin-A. It strengthens immunity, supports skin health, and aids digestion due to its high fiber content. Low in fat, often recommended in weight loss diets. It is anti-inflammatory and mildly laxative. Antioxidants, carotenoids and flavonoids help regulate blood sugar and support diabetic diets in moderation.

plants.name: Jackfruit
plants.origin: Indo-Malaysia region, particularly Western Ghats, Southeast Asia including Vietnam
plants.economicUse: Ripe fruits are eaten fresh or used in desserts, ice cream and beverages. Unripe fruits are cooked as vegetables or meat substitutes. Seeds are roasted or boiled. Used in processed foods such as chips, canned jackfruit, jams and syrups. Wood is used for furniture and musical instruments. Latex is traditionally used as an adhesive.
plants.vedicSignificance: Jackfruit (Panasa) is well documented in Ayurveda. Classical texts describe it as nourishing, strengthening and cooling. Fruits, seeds, leaves and bark are used for balancing Vata and Pitta. Mentioned in Charaka Samhita and Sushruta Samhita.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in fiber, antioxidants and Vitamin-C. Supports digestion, boosts immunity and helps reduce inflammation. Rich in potassium for blood pressure regulation. Seeds have aphrodisiac properties in Ayurveda. Latex and bark are traditionally used for wound healing and skin diseases. Possesses anti-ulcer and antibacterial properties.

plants.name: White Sapota
plants.vernacularName: White Sapota / Casimiroa / Mexican Apple / Zapote Blanco
plants.origin: Central America and Mexico
plants.economicUse: Fruits are creamy with sweet custard-like pulp. Consumed fresh or used in smoothies, ice creams and desserts. Grown in orchards and backyard gardens. Popular in tropical and subtropical regions and increasingly cultivated for gourmet fruit markets.
plants.medicalSignificance: White Sapota is traditionally used as a mild sedative to calm nerves and aid sleep. Rich in Vitamin-C and Vitamin-A, supports immunity and eye health. Helps digestion and gut health. Traditionally used for blood sugar regulation. Anti-inflammatory and antioxidant. Rich potassium content supports healthy blood pressure.

plants.name: Avocado
plants.origin: Central America and Southern Mexico
plants.economicUse: Fresh fruit is rich and creamy. Used in salads, toast, smoothies and guacamole. Avocado oil is widely used in culinary, cosmetic and pharmaceutical products. Used in nutraceuticals. Seeds and peels are researched for antioxidant properties. It is an important export crop in tropical and subtropical countries.
plants.medicalSignificance: Avocado supports heart health through healthy monounsaturated fats and potassium. Helps lower bad cholesterol and regulate blood pressure. Rich in Vitamin-E, polyphenols, fiber, folate and Vitamin-K. Supports skin, hair, digestion, brain and bone health. Possesses antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antibacterial and potential anti-diabetic properties.

plants.name: Lubika Sunny Sweet
plants.vernacularName: Lubika Sunny Sweet / Indian Coffee Plum
plants.origin: Tropical Asia, most likely India/Southeast Asia
plants.economicUse: Fresh fruits are eaten raw, made into pickles, chutneys, jams, marmalade, and curries. It is grown as hedge plants and sold as saplings for home orchards. Its wood is occasionally harvested for lumber.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in antioxidants and antimicrobial compounds, useful in managing oxidative stress and infections. Anti-diabetic, helps lower blood glucose levels. Supports digestion, relieves constipation, promotes cardiovascular health, and has traditional uses for arthritis and memory enhancement.

plants.name: Madroño
plants.origin: Tropical Americas — particularly Trinidad, Central and South Tropical America including Colombia
plants.economicUse: Fruits are consumed fresh, known for their sweet to slightly citrusy pulp with a foamy texture. Occasionally cultivated and also used as animal feed and fuelwood.
plants.medicalSignificance: Possesses antioxidative and anti-inflammatory effects. Extracts show antimicrobial and antiplatelet activity. It is hypoglycemic, antihyperlipidemic, hepatoprotective and cardioprotective. Xanthones present in the fruit exhibit anticancer, neuroprotective and metabolic benefits.

plants.name: Luc's Mexican Garcinia
plants.vernacularName: Luc's Mexican Garcinia / Mexican Mangosteen / Limoncillo
plants.origin: Mexico
plants.economicUse: Fruits are sweet with a lemony-tart flavour. Fruit is used as a weight-loss medicine. It is cultivated in fruit gardens and grown as a slow shade-loving tree.
plants.medicalSignificance: Fruit is used in weight management due to its ability to reduce appetite and inhibit fat synthesis through hydroxycitric acid. Used traditionally as an astringent for dysentery and digestive complaints. May help regulate blood sugar and cholesterol. Bark and resin are used as cathartic and purgative medicines.

plants.name: Kei Apple
plants.origin: Southern Africa, particularly Mozambique and South Africa
plants.economicUse: Fruits are edible, tart to yellow-orange, used in jams, jellies, preserves and beverages. Plants are commonly grown as protective hedges because of their dense thorny branches and are also used for ornamental landscaping.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in Vitamin-C, supports immunity and acts as an antioxidant. Exhibits antibacterial properties and may help in managing infections. Traditionally used for digestive health, mild laxative effects and treatment of skin ailments.

plants.name: Red/Pink Water Apple
plants.origin: Southeast Asia, particularly Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Andaman & Nicobar Islands
plants.economicUse: Fruit is eaten fresh and used in fruit salads, pickles, juices and traditional sweets. Crisp and mildly sweet. It is also grown as an ornamental tree due to its glossy leaves and attractive fruits. Commonly used in agroforestry and tropical landscaping.
plants.medicalSignificance: Fruits are rich in water and fiber, aiding hydration and digestion. Low in calories, making them suitable for weight management. Rich in antioxidants and possess mild diuretic properties supporting kidney and urinary health. Traditionally used for fever, liver health and skin care in several cultures.

plants.name: Custard apple
plants.origin: Tropical South America particularly Brazil, Peru, and the Amazon Basin
plants.economicUse: Fresh fruit is edible, soft, creamy, sweet-sour flesh used in desserts, milkshakes, or ice creams. It is an orchard crop,  grown in tropical fruit orchards; gaining popularity in exotic fruit markets.
plants.medicalSignificance: Custard apple is rich in Vitamin-C and B-complex – supports immune function and energy metabolism. It is antioxidant and anti-inflammatory – potential for reducing oxidative stress and inflammation. It has mild sedative properties. It has digestive aid – high in fiber, supports gut health. It is traditionally used to treat fever, diarrhea, and as a natural energy booster.

plants.name: Nance fruit
plants.origin: Tropical America particularly Mexico to northern South America and the Caribbean
plants.economicUse: Edible fruit is consumed raw, or used in desserts, candies, drinks, fermented beverages (like chicha), jams. It is occasionally used for firewood or small-scale timber. Trees are used in reforestation & landscaping, tolerant to poor soils and drought.
plants.medicalSignificance: Fruits are rich in water and fiber, aid in hydration and digestion. Fruit is low calorie – suitable for weight management. Rich in antioxidant properties – may help reduce oxidative stress. It has diuretic effects thus used to support kidney and urinary.

plants.name: Sundrop layered
plants.origin: Northwestern South America (Ecuador, Colombia, Peru)
plants.economicUse: Fruit is edible bright orange with green pulp; used in juices, jams, sauces, and desserts. It is a commercial fruit crop especially in Ecuador and Colombia for fresh market and juice industry. The export value is high.
plants.medicalSignificance: Fruit is rich in Vitamin-C and Iron, boosts immunity and blood health. It is rich in antioxidants, helps fight free radicals. It is diuretic & detoxifying, used to cleanse kidneys and liver. It is anti-inflammatory & Digestive Aid – juice is soothing and supports digestion. It has been traditinally used for hypertension, cholesterol, and weight management in folk medicine.

plants.name: Cowa fruit
plants.origin: South and Southeast Asia (India, Thailand, Myanmar, Malaysia, Indonesia)
plants.economicUse: Fruits are eaten fresh or cooked; used in curries, pickles, and preserves for its sour taste. Acts as a substitute for tamarind in many Southeast Asian dishes. Yellow dye from the bark used in traditional textiles. Used as timber & fuelwood.  Used as an ornamental plant for its glossy leaves and attractive canopy.
plants.medicalSignificance: It is a digestive stimulant, promotes appetite and digestion. It is antimicrobial & antiparasitic, traditionally used to treat infections, diarrhea, and intestinal worms. It is anti-inflammatory, fruit  and bark used for swelling and pain relief.  Decoctions from the bark used as a hepatoprotective tonic. Used in Thai and Indian folk medicine to aid uterine recovery.

plants.name: Kepple fruit
plants.origin: Malesia, especially cultivated in Java, Indonesia
plants.economicUse: Keppal is valued as an ornamental and symbol of identity (e.g. the Yogyakarta region). It is traditionally used as oral deodorant, body scent enhancer, contraceptive; used by palace women in Java for centuries.
plants.medicalSignificance: Fruit, seeds, roots contain saponins, flavonoids, polyphenols, alkaloids, quercetin, and other antioxidants like terpenes and vitami C/E. Natural deodorant – reduces body odor in sweat and urine by suppressing odor-causing compounds. Kidney support & diuretic – promotes urine flow, helps prevent inflammation and deposits in kidney. Gout relief – alkaloid content helps neutralize pH and reduce joint inflammation. Anti‑cancer/ anti‑tumor activity – acetogenins, styryl lactones, isoflavones may inhibit cancer cell growth and encourage apoptosis. Liver protection (hepatoprotective) – capable of restoring liver enzyme production and supporting cell regeneration. Skin / cell regeneration – antioxidants support skin health, blood purification and promote youthful vitality.

plants.name: Olosapo fruit hybrid
plants.origin: Mexico through Central America (including Guatemala, Belize, Costa Rica, El Salvador, and Honduras)
plants.economicUse: Fresh fruit is pureed into smoothies, desserts, ice cream, jams, sauces; pairs well with fruits like banana, coconut, strawberry and flavors like chocolate, vanilla, nutmeg
plants.medicalSignificance: High in dietary fiber, supporting digestion and detoxification. Contains vitamin C and antioxidants that may support immunity, collagen formation, reduce inflammation. Limited phytochemistry documented: compounds like oleanolic acid, betulinic acid, stigmasterol and a novel triterpene have been isolated, inhibiting DNA polymerase β lyase activity in vitro.

plants.name: Nam Nam fruit
plants.vernacularName: Nam Nam fruit / Kata Puru, Puki Anjing / Buah Katak Puru
plants.origin: Indo-Malaya region. Peninsular Malaysia; also found in Sri Lanka, India, Indonesia
plants.economicUse: Sour when unripe; mild, sweet‑tangy when ripe—likened to unripe apple or carambola; crunchy-fibrous pulp used in jams, jellies, beverages, juices.
plants.medicalSignificance:
High vitamin C and A, antioxidants, polyphenols, flavonoids; ~87% water; fiber, protein, carbs. Diabetes & Hypertension: Leaf decoctions and young shoots are traditionally used to manage blood sugar and high blood pressure.
Skin health: Seed oil is applied topically in parts of India to treat skin conditions like rashes and infections. Digestive health / diuretic: Fruit and leaves are used in folk remedies for digestive discomfort, urinary flow, and as mild diuretic agents.

plants.name: Wetland abiurana
plants.origin: Wetlands of the Amazon Basin. Neotropical, especially Brazilian Amazon floodplain forests
plants.economicUse: Regarded as a forest delicacy; shared during harvest in indigenous Amazon communities. Fruits are eaten fresh, juiced, or in sweet pulp preparations, sometimes blended into smoothies or desserts.
plants.medicalSignificance: itamin C & B₃ (Niacin): Supports immune function, skin health, energy metabolism, and nervous system function. Antioxidants and dietary fiber: Aid digestion, reduce oxidative stress, support gut health, may protect against chronic diseases . Anti‑Inflammatory and digestive seu. Reported to relieve mild respiratory complaints, reduce fatigue, alleviate arthritis symptoms, and promote general well-being.

plants.name: Davidson plum (Davidson plum)
plants.origin: Subtropical rainforest of Northern New South Wales & Queensland, Australia
plants.economicUse: Culinary uses include jams, sauces, chutneys, ice creams, sorbets, cordials, wines, and spice-infused desserts. They’re often used in powdered or freeze‑dried form, adding a vivid color and tart flavor to sweet and savory dishes.
plants.medicalSignificance:
Extremely high levels of anthocynin, greater than blueberries—offering potent antioxidant activity. These pigments support eye, brain, heart, and immune health. Vitamin C, Vitamin E, Zinc, Calcium, Magnesium, Folate, Lutein, plus a favorable potassium-to-sodium ratio. High anthocyanins and polyphenols may reduce oxidative stress, support cardiovascular health, and inhibit inflammation associated with chronic diseases including metabolic disorders and neurodegeneration. Metabolic and Cardiovascular Support: Studies show reductions in visceral fat, plasma triglycerides, blood pressure, inflammatory cell infiltration in heart/liver, and improved tissue integrity in obesity models—especially linked to D. pruriens. 
Immune and Skin Health: Vitamin E, zinc, lutein, and antioxidants contribute to skin repair, UV protection, collagen synthesis, immune support, and eye health.  Digestive Benefits: With fiber content and mild laxative properties, Davidson plum may support digestive regularity and beneficial gut flora.

plants.name: Mexican Black Plum
plants.origin: Mexico & Central America, including Belize, Guatemala, Honduras
plants.economicUse: High pectin content makes it ideal for jelly, jam, and ponche. Sweet sour fruit helps in making sauces, preserves, drinks, marinades, salsas, and desserts.  Used in living fences and agroforestry systems, and sap/bark as glue or traditional resin for treating jaundice among indigenous groups.
plants.medicalSignificance:
Antioxidant & anti-inflammatory action: anthocyanins and polyphenols may reduce oxidative stress and inflammation; support digestive and cardiovascular health.
Digestive health: Fiber and pectin aid in constipation relief, promote gut health, and help regulate cholesterol and blood sugar. Immunity & skin health: Vitamin C contributes to immune support and skin repair; folklore uses include applying crushed leaves/bark to irritated skin or wounds. Crushed fruit or leaves applied to relieve headache, muscle pain, and ulcers/sores, including canker sores.

plants.name: Mulberry var long, short
plants.origin: Tibet, the Himalayas, Indochina; found across India, Bhutan, Myanmar, and Southeast Asia
plants.economicUse: Eaten raw, used in jams, juices; cultivated for large fruit yield (hundreds of pounds per tree); leaves used for sericulture (silkworm feed); wood quality suited for furniture and small construction uses.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in phenolic compounds and flavonoids. Anti‑ulcer & anti‑inflammatory potential. It has neuroprotective & anticancer activity.

plants.name: Golden Custard Apple
plants.origin: Tropical and subtropical regions; this golden variant is cultivated in India, particularly Maharashtra
plants.economicUse: Consumed fresh, blended into smoothies, desserts, ice-creams, jams, and milkshakes.
plants.medicalSignificance:
Immunity & Skin: Rich in vitamin C and antioxidants; helps in free-radical scavenging, skin elasticity, wound healing, and enhancing collagen synthesis. Digestive Support: Dietary fiber promotes regularity, nourishes gut microbiota, may help control blood sugar by slowing sugar absorption. Anti-diabetic & Anti-inflammatory: The high fiber and phytonutrient content supports glycemic regulation and reduces inflammation, beneficial in managing arthritis symptoms.
Hair & Eye Health: Vitamin C supports hair strength, combats dandruff and includes limited beta-carotene for eye protection and age-related macular degeneration prevention.

plants.name: Sweet Plum
plants.origin: Europe and Central Asia; widely cultivated worldwide
plants.economicUse: Eaten fresh, dried into prunes, made into jams, juices, sauces, baked goods, preserves, and fermented beverages.
plants.vedicSignificance: Plums are historically noted for their cooling, sweet-sour and astringent nature when ripe. They are used to balance Pitta and Kapha dosha in traditional descriptions. Seed powder and fruit extracts used in Ayurveda to manage diabetes due to jambosine compound. Used to treat diarrhea, dysentery, cough, asthma, gum disorders, nausea, throat pain, and seasonal Pitta-related ailments.
plants.medicalSignificance:
Digestive health: High soluble fiber and sorbitol content help relieve constipation, support gut motility, and improve stool consistency. Heart & metabolic support: Potassium and antioxidants help regulate blood pressure and lipid profiles; fiber moderates post-meal blood sugar spikes.
Antioxidant & Anti-inflammatory: Phenolic compounds and anthocyanins help reduce oxidative stress and inflammation; may lower risk of chronic conditions like diabetes and neurodegeneration. Bone health: Dried plums (prunes) provide vitamin K and phenolics that may help prevent bone loss, especially in postmenopausal women. Skin & Eye health: Vitamins A and C, lutein/zeaxanthin support skin repair, collagen production, and vision health. Immune support & anemia prevention: Vitamin C with iron aids absorption and supports healthy hemoglobin levels.

plants.name: Blue Sabara
plants.vernacularName: Blue Sabara / Blue Grape / False Jaboticaba
plants.origin: South America—Costa Rica, Panama to Venezuela; Sabará hybrid traced to Brazil
plants.economicUse: Consumed fresh, juiced, fermented into wines or jams; also valued in ornamental horticulture and container gardening due to manageable size and attractive bark/leaves.
plants.medicalSignificance: Oxidative & inflammatory protection: Anthocyanins and polyphenols may reduce inflammation, benefit cardiovascular and metabolic health. Vision & skin support: Vitamins A/C/E, zinc, selenium support eye health, collagen synthesis, UV protection, and immune function. Bone health: Minerals like calcium, phosphorus, magnesium contribute to bone formation and density.

plants.name: Camu Camu
plants.origin: Amazonian floodplain regions—Peru, Brazil, Colombia, Bolivia, Venezuela
plants.economicUse: Primarily processed into powders, juices, purees, or capsules. Also used commercially in foods, supplements, desserts, and cosmetic products globally (especially Japan).
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in fiber, potassium, manganese, calcium, magnesium, iron, flavonoids, anthocyanins, carotenoids like lutein, ellagic and gallic acids. mmune support & antioxidant power: Combination of vitamin C and polyphenols more effective against oxidative stress than vitamin C alone; shown to reduce C-reactive protein and IL‑6 in smokers. Anti-inflammatory: Phenolic compounds deliver potent activity; animal and human studies suggest inflammation reduction beyond vitamin C alone. Metabolic & weight support: Preliminary animal studies indicate improved weight control and metabolic syndrome markers; human data limited but promising. Blood sugar & antidiabetic action: Extracts shown to inhibit α-amylase and α-glucosidase, reducing post-meal glucose spikes; human trials indicate lowered glucose levels.

plants.name: Rose Sapote
plants.origin: Central America; introduced and cultivated in Florida and tropical/subtropical gardens
plants.economicUse: Used fresh, blended into smoothies, desserts, ice creams, pies, jams, juices, preserves. Also valued as ornamental fruit tree.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in vitamin A and vitamin C, dietary fiber, potassium; may contain carotenoids like beta-carotene and other antioxidants. Digestive aid: Smooth, easily digestible pulp; cooling and gentle on stomach; high beta-carotene and mucilage help soothe gastritis, heartburn, diarrhea. Antioxidant & Anti-inflammatory: Vitamin C, tannins, polyphenols protect against oxidative stress, support skin and immune health. Skin & hair health: Oil from seeds (called sapayul or sapote oil) used in cosmetics and as hair tonic; folk use includes applying seed kernel oil or powder to stop hair fall and treat dandruff; also used as sedative and skin healing agent. Antimicrobial & wound care: Extracts from flower and leaves show in vitro antibacterial activity; roasted seed powder used as poultice for wounds, cough, asthma.

plants.name: Sweet Purple Surinam Cherry
plants.vernacularName: Sweet Purple Surinam Cherry / Pitanga, Brazilian Cherry, Cayenne Cherry
plants.origin: Eastern Tropical South America—Suriname, French Guiana, Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay, Argentina.
plants.economicUse: Eaten fresh only when fully ripe; also processed into jams, jellies, sauces, juices, wines, syrups, pickles; ornamental hedge widely grown in tropical gardens.
plants.medicalSignificance:
Immunomodulatory & Skin Health: Vitami C and antioxidants support immunity, collagen synthesis, and skin protection from UV damage. Anti-inflammatory / Antioxidant: Polyphenols and anthocyanins reduce inflammation and oxidative stress, possibly lowering risks of cardiovascular and chronic diseases. Digestive & Metabolic Support: Dietary fiber aids digestion, prevents constipation, may help regulate cholesterol and blood sugar; preliminary research suggests hypoglycemic effects.
Antimicrobial / Antifungal: Leaf and fruit extracts (and essential oils) show activity against bacteria and fungi; also tested in vitro against parasites like Leishmania, Trypanosoma and trichomonads.

plants.name: Sweet Mundu Fruit
plants.vernacularName: Sweet Mundu Fruit / Egg Tree / Mundu / Baniti / Rata Fruit
plants.origin: Native to Southeast Asia—Indonesia (Java, Borneo), Philippines, Thailand, Malaysia.
plants.economicUse: Edible raw when ripe, but most commonly used in juices, jams, chutneys, or preserves owing to its sweet–acidic balance and aromatic pulp.
plants.medicalSignificance: Wound healing & anti-inflammatory: Pulp or juice is applied topically to minor cuts, sprains, and inflammation, accelerating healing and easing pain. Digestive support: Used traditionally for abdominal discomfort, gastritis, bile issues, and to promote bowel movement (relieves constipation). Goiter & bile disorders: Some folk remedies recommend sprinkling dried pulp on the affected area for goiter; fresh pulp taken to assist bile-related symptoms .

plants.name: Tataruba Fruit
plants.origin: Brazil
plants.economicUse: Consumed fresh, also processed into jams, jellies, syrups, juices, and wines. Popular in ornamental and edible landscaping for its fruit and showy branching.
plants.medicalSignificance: Contains vitami C, anthocyanins, polyphenols, flavonoids, and dietary fiber, offering strong antioxidant potential. Antioxidant & anti-inflammatory: May support cardiovascular and metabolic health through reduction of free radicals. Digestive support: Fiber content aids digestion; juice or pulp may refresh and cleanse. Immune support & skin care: Vitamin C and phenolics support immunity, skin regeneration, and collagen formation.

plants.name: Acai Berry
plants.origin: Amazon region
plants.economicUse: it’s processed into frozen pulp, juices, smoothie bowls (açaí na tigela), supplements, and cosmetic ingreditents.
plants.medicalSignificance: Contains vitamin A (especially in extract form), minimal vitamin C, fiber, protein, and heart-healthy fats. Rich in anthocyanins (cyanidin-3-glucoside, cyanidin-3-rutinoside), flavonoids (quercetin, catechins), phenolic acids such as vanillic, ferulic, protocatechuic, and syringic acid. Antioxidant & anti-inflammatory effects. Acai extracts reduce oxidative stress, inflammation markers, and neuronal damage in studies simulating Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease. Cardiometabolic health. Neuroprotective & cognitive support.

plants.name: Uvalha
plants.origin: Brazil – especially the Atlantic Forest biome
plants.economicUse: Food Industry: Eaten raw (by those who enjoy its strong taste. Used in juices, jellies, ice creams, and liqueurs in Brazil. Rich in vitamin C and antioxidants. Agroforestry and Reforestation: Planted in reforestation projects in Brazil due to its ecological value. Attracts pollinators and wildlife. Timber: Wood used locally for small construction and firewood.
plants.medicalSignificance: Antioxidant properties (high in polyphenols and vitamin C). Anti-inflammatory activity. Digestive benefits: due to its acidity and fiber content. Antimicrobial properties: from essential oils found in the leaves and fruit peel.

plants.name: Surinam Cherry var. Black Star
plants.origin: South America – mainly Brazil, Suriname, and Uruguay
plants.economicUse: Eaten fresh, made into jellies, jams, juices, sauces, and wines. Grown as hedge, bonsai, or ornamental tree due to its glossy foliage. Used in tropical and subtropical gardens; drought-tolerant species.
plants.medicalSignificance: Antioxidant & Anti-inflammatory - Due to high polyphenol and vitamin C content. Antimicrobial- Leaf extracts show activity against bacteria and fungi. Digestive aid - Fruit used to relieve stomach issues and aid bowel movement. Astringent properties - Leaves used in teas or poultices for skin or digestive issues. Anti-diabetic - Folk use for blood sugar control; some studies suggest mild activity.

plants.name: Yellow Jaboticaba
plants.origin: Brazil, especially the Atlantic Forest biome
plants.economicUse: Eaten fresh; also used in jellies, juices, wines, and liqueurs. Grown as an exotic fruit tree in gardens and collections. Used in biodiversity gardens and reforestation projects.
plants.medicalSignificance: Antioxidant	Rich in vitamin C, polyphenols, and flavonoids. Anti-inflammatory - Leaf and fruit extracts reported to have anti-inflammatory effects. Digestive aid - Traditionally consumed to improve digestion. Antimicrobial - Early studies suggest inhibition of bacterial growth.

plants.name: Matoa
plants.origin: Southeast Asia and Pacific Islands — native to Papua New Guinea, Indonesia, and parts of Melanesia
plants.economicUse: Fruits are consumed fresh, used in juices or traditional snacks. Timberwood is highly valued for furniture and construction. Agroforestry -- grown in multi-use tropical orchards, home gardens
plants.medicalSignificance: Antioxidant	Fruit rich in vitamins (especially vitamin C) and polyphenols. Anti-inflammatory-Traditionally used to reduce swelling or pain. Antibacterial- some studies show leaf and bark extracts inhibit microbial growth. Cooling effect - In traditional Indonesian/Malay herbal practice, the fruit is thought to cool the body. Digestive benefits	- Light, fiber-rich pulp aids digestion.

plants.name: Icecream Beans
plants.origin: Amazon rainforest, native to Central and South America
plants.economicUse: Eaten fresh, sweet pulp used in juices or desserts. Nitrogen-fixing tree used in permaculture and reforestation/agroforestry projects. Commonly used to provide shade in coffee/cacao plantations. Timberwood used for light construction and firewood
plants.medicalSignificance: Anti-inflammatory- Traditional use of bark for inflammation and pain. Antioxidant- Pulp is rich in vitamin C and polyphenols. Antimicrobial- Extracts from leaves and bark studied for antibacterial properties. Blood sugar control- Some traditional systems use it to manage diabetes-like conditions. Digestive aid- Pulp is light, fibrous, and mildly laxative.

plants.name: Makhota Dewa
plants.vernacularName: Makhota Dewa / God’s Crown Fruit / Crown of God
plants.origin: Indonesia, specifically the Papua region, and is also found in Malaysia
plants.economicUse: Eaten fresh, used in folk / traditional medicine for remedies.
plants.medicalSignificance: Treats diabetes, high blood pressure, gout, kidney inflammation, and allergies. Rich in flavonoids (such as quercetin), alkaloids, tannins, saponins, and phenolics—these contribute to its antioxidant, anti‑gout, anti‑hypertensive, antimicrobial and anticancer potential.

plants.name: Pomelo
plants.origin: Southeast Asia, particularly Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and southern China
plants.economicUse: Eaten fresh or used in salads, juices, jams, and desserts. Exported as a fresh fruit from tropical and subtropical countries. Juice and rind are used in flavoring, candied peel production, and beverages. Essential oils from the peel are used in perfumes and cosmetic products.
plants.medicalSignificance:
Rich in Antioxidants: Contains vitamin C, flavonoids, and polyphenols, which help reduce oxidative stress. Boosts Immunity: High vitamin C content supports immune health. Aids Digestion: Dietary fiber improves gut health and relieves constipation.
Heart Health: Helps lower blood pressure and cholesterol due to potassium and antioxidant content. Weight Management: Low in calories, high in water and fiber — helpful in weight loss diets. Anti-inflammatory & Antimicrobial: Extracts from the peel and seeds show potential antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory effects.

plants.name: Alligator pepper
plants.origin: West Africa, especially countries like Nigeria, Ghana, Cameroon, and Liberia.
plants.economicUse: Used as a spice in African cuisine for adding to soups, stews, and local beverages, it is spicy with a peppery, ginger-like flavor. Has very high export value.
plants.medicalSignificance: Antimicrobial Properties: Contains compounds that inhibit bacterial and fungal growth. Anti-inflammatory & Analgesic: Helps reduce inflammation and relieve pain. Digestive Aid: Stimulates digestion and relieves stomach discomfort and bloating. Aphrodisiac Effects: Traditionally believed to enhance libido and sexual performance. Antioxidant Activity: Rich in flavonoids and tannins which combat oxidative stress. Antidiabetic Potential: Studies suggest it may help lower blood sugar levels. Wound Healing: Applied traditionally to wounds and cuts to promote healing. It is functionally similar to long pepper (Pippali).

plants.name: Israel Orange Kumquat
plants.origin: South China
plants.economicUse: Eaten fresh and whole, popular for its unique flavor – sweet skin and tart flesh. Used in jams, jellies, marmalades, liqueurs, candies, and syrups. Grown commercially in Israel, China, and USA, especially for niche fruit markets. Compact trees with glossy leaves and bright orange fruit thus cultivated in gardens and landscaping.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in Vitamin C: Boosts immunity and improves skin health. Antioxidant-Rich: contains flavonoids, carotenoids, and essential oils with anti-inflammatory and anti-aging properties. Aids Digestion: High fiber content supports gut health and prevents constipation. Controls Blood Sugar: Low glycemic index; polyphenols may help regulate sugar metabolism. upports Heart Health: Potassium and antioxidants reduce blood pressure and oxidative stress. Natural Antimicrobial: Peel extracts have shown antimicrobial activity against certain pathogens.

plants.name: Dragon fruit
plants.origin: Central America and northern South America, particularly Mexico, Guatemala, and Costa Rica
plants.economicUse: Fresh Market Fruit: Popular for its vibrant color, unique appearance, and mildly sweet taste. Consumed fresh, in smoothies, fruit bowls, or desserts. Major export fruit for Vietnam, Thailand, and Israel. Processed Products: Used in juices, jams, ice cream, and nutraceuticals. Natural Colorant: The red-fleshed variety is used as a natural food dye due to its high betalain content. Ornamental Use: Grown as an ornamental climbing cactus in gardens.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in Antioxidants: Contains vitamin C, betalains, and polyphenols. Boosts Immunity: High vitamin C and minerals like iron and zinc support immune functionDigestive Health: High in dietary fiber and prebiotic compounds (oligosaccharides). Regulates Blood Sugar: Low glycemic index and beneficial for type 2 diabetes. Heart Health: Contains monounsaturated fats (from seeds) and fiber to lower cholesterol.

plants.name: Kanta Kachur
plants.origin: Indo-Malaya region. Found widely in India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Vietnam, Malaysia, and Indonesia
plants.economicUse: Eaten as vegetable. Young shoots, leaves, and rhizomes are consumed as a green leafy vegetable. Cooked to reduce acridity (due to calcium oxalate crystals). Popular in Sri Lankan and northeastern Indian cuisine. Used as livestock feed in some rural areas. The mature stems and roots are sometimes used in rural crafts or for tying because of their fibrous nature.
plants.medicalSignificance: Anti-inflammatory and Antioxidant: Contains phenolic compounds that reduce inflammation and oxidative stress. Antimicrobial Properties: Extracts show antibacterial and antifungal activities. Digestive Aid: Used to treat constipation, indigestion, and worm infestations. Diuretic Effect: Helps in promoting urination and detoxification. It is anti-diabetic.

plants.name: Durian
plants.origin: Indo-Malaya region particularly Malaysia, Indonesia, and Brunei
plants.economicUse: Durian is called as King of Fruits. Eaten fresh, or used in ice cream, cakes, candies. Eaten raw, processed into desserts and snacks, major export. Durian paste, powder, and freeze-dried snacks are popular globally. Seeds are cooked and eaten in some regions.
plants.medicalSignificance: High in carbohydrates, healthy fats, dietary fiber, and vitamins B1, B6, C, and potassium. Calorie-dense; often used for energy and strength. It is antioxidant & anti-inflammatory: Rich in flavonoids, polyphenols, and organosulfur compounds with anti-aging and anti-inflammatory properties. Contains potassium, magnesium, and copper, supporting cardiovascular and skeletal health. Good prebiotic properties due to fiber and oligosaccharides. Aphrodisiac: in southeast Asian folklore, it is considered to increase libido.

plants.name: Litchi
plants.origin: Southern China, Northern Vietnam, and parts of Southeast Asia
plants.economicUse:
Litchi is eaten raw/fresh for its juicy, sweet, aromatic pulp. Used in juices, squashes, jams, canned syrups, ice creams, and jellies.
Exported from India, China, Thailand, Vietnam to Gulf, Europe, and North America. Major fruit in commercial orchards, especially in Bihar (Muzaffarpur), a GI-tagged region for Shahi Litchi.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in Antioxidants: Contains vitamin C, polyphenols, and flavonoids that boost immunity and fight oxidative stress. Supports Digestion: Contains soluble fiber aiding bowel health. Anti-inflammatory and Antiviral: Exhibits protective effects against certain viruses and inflammation. Cardiovascular Health: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure. Weight Management: Low calorie, fat-free, and hydrating—good for summer diets. Seed Extracts: Traditionally used for diabetes management and liver protection

plants.name: Bilva
plants.origin: Indian subcontinent (Eastern Ghats) and spread across South and Southeast Asia, including Sri Lanka and Thailand
plants.economicUse:
resh fruit eaten or processed into sharbats, juices, murabba (preserved fruit), toffee, pulp powders, syrups, and desserts. Popular summer drink "Bela Pana" uses bael pulp mixed with milk and spices. 
Medicinal Preparations: Used in traditional formulations across Ayurvedic, Siddha, and Unani systems. All parts fruit, leaves, bark, seeds, roots—are used for therapeutic preparations Culturally & Religiously sacred to Lord Shiva; bael leaves are used in temple rituals and religious offerings.
plants.vedicSignificance: Recognized in Ayurveda & classical texts as Bilva or Bel, highly sacred and medicinal. Frequently mentioned in Charaka Samhita, Sushruta, and Bhavaprakasha for its dosha-balancing and therapeutic functions. Ayurvedic Properties: Rasa (Taste): Madhura (sweet), Tikta (bitter), Katu (pungent). Guna (Quality): Laghu (light), Ruksha (dry). Virya (Potency): Ushna (hot, Vipaka: Katu (pungent after digestion). It balances Vata and Kapha; reduces Pitta.
plants.medicalSignificance:
Rich in Phytochemicals: contains fiber, carotenoids, phenolics, terpenoids, coumarins, flavonoids, alkaloids (e.g. aegeline, marmeline), tannins, and sterols.
Digestive Health: Fruit pulp supports relief from constipation, diarrhea, and indigestion. Anti-inflammatory, Antimicrobial, Antioxidant: Leaf, bark, and fruit extracts exhibit strong activities against inflammation, oxidative stress, bacterial and fungal infections. Metabolic & Liver Support: Used in treatments for diabetes, jaundice, liver disorders, and urinary conditions. Cardiovascular health: Promotes heart health and may help in managing blood pressure. It helps in wound healing & skin disorders.

plants.name: Santol
plants.vernacularName: Santol / Wild Mangosteen / Cotton Fruit / Lolly Fruit
plants.origin: Indochina and Malesian region (Malaysia, Indonesia, Philippines)
plants.economicUse:
Santol's fleshy pulp (white or red) around seeds is sweet to sour, often eaten fresh or with salt/spices. Santol is used in making jams, jellies, preserves, pickles, chutneys, and syrup. It is used in Filipino cuisine (e.g., sinantolan). The tree provides durable wood, used for construction, furniture, and tools.
 The bark, leaves, roots, and fruit used in local remedies across Southeast Asia and Sri Lanka.
plants.medicalSignificance: Antibacterial and Antifungal: Bark and leaves show activity against Staphylococcus and E. coli. Digestive Aid: Traditionally used to treat diarrhea, stomach upset, and intestinal worms. Skin Conditions: Leaf and bark decoctions used for eczema, rashes, and insect bites. Anti-inflammatory and Analgesic: Roots and bark decoction used to relieve pain and inflammation. Liver and Metabolic Benefits: Fruit extract may help with cholesterol control and detoxification.

plants.name: Sweet Orange
plants.origin: Southern China and Northeastern India
plants.economicUse: Fruit Consumption: Most popular citrus fruit globally; eaten fresh or juiced. Processed Products: Juice concentrate, candied peel, jams, marmalades, flavored beverages, desserts, and confectionery. Essential Oils: Extracted from peel and flower for use in aromatherapy, cosmetics, cleaners, and perfumery. It is a major export commodity especially from Brazil, USA, and India. Citrus peels used to produce pectin, bioflavonoids, and cattle feed additives.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in Vitamin C: Strengthens immune system, boosts collagen production, and supports iron absorption. Digestive Aid: High in dietary fiber (pectin), improves digestion and relieves constipation. Cardiovascular Health: Contains flavonoids (hesperidin, naringenin) beneficial for heart and blood vessels. Antioxidant & Anti-inflammatory: Reduces oxidative stress and inflammation. Skin & Hair Health: Juice and peel help reduce acne, pigmentation; promotes healthy skin and hair. Weight and Blood Sugar Control: Low glycemic index, rich in fiber, helps in weight management and blood sugar regulation.

plants.name: Jagma Cherry
plants.origin: South Asia, including India, especially southern and eastern regions
plants.economicUse: Fruits eaten fresh, or processed into jams, marmalades, pickles, sweets, and occasionally vinegars. In Kerala, coffee plum jam is widespread and marketed for domestic and export markets. Fruits and leaves used in traditional dishes, sauces, or as souring agents in small-scale homemade recipes. Wood is occasionally used for lumber.
plants.medicalSignificance: Digestive Aid & Antidiarrheal: Both fruit and leaves are traditionally used to treat diarrhea and dysentery. Antifungal & Antibacterial: Bark and leaves have shown activity against fungal and bacterial pathogens, used topically or in decoctions. Used as a tonic for bronchitis, toothache, and other minor ailments. It is a anthelmintic, purgative, diuretic, expectorant, antipyretic, hepatoprotective, analgesic.

plants.name: Tropical Apricot
plants.origin: Tropical Asia, Sri Lanka and Southern India
plants.economicUse: Fruits are used for: Fresh consumption (though tart, some cultivars are sweeter). Juices, jams, jellies, and preserves. Flavoring agents: Sometimes used as rootstock or hedge plant due to its spiny nature. It is rich in vitamin C, antioxidants, and has nutraceutical value.
plants.medicalSignificance: Used in digestive tonics and immunity boosters. Possible use for skin issues, scurvy, or as a mild laxative. Antioxidant activity: The fruit is rich in vitamin C, polyphenols, and flavonoids. These compounds help neutralize free radicals, potentially preventing oxidative stress-related condition. It helps in cardiovascular diseases. It helps in premature aging. It is anti-cancerous. It is a good digestive tonic.

plants.name: Susang Kalabau
plants.origin: Native to Philippines extending through Malesia, Cambodia, Thailand, New Guinea, and northern Australia
plants.economicUse: Wood is used as a rattan substitute in furniture and handicraft valued in restoration efforts.
plants.medicalSignificance: Information currently unavailable.

plants.name: Sweet lime
plants.origin: India or Indo‑Burma
plants.economicUse: Sweet lime is commonly consumed mainly as fresh fruit, juice (most popular use). It is used fro making soft drinks, sherbets, and refreshing drinks, pickles and traditional chutneys (regionally).
plants.vedicSignificance: Mentioned in Ayurveda as Madhuphala, Madhurima, sometimes simply under Nimbu variants. Rasa (taste): Madhura (sweet) with a hint of amla (sour). Guna: Laghu (light), Snigdha (unctuous). Virya: Sheeta (cooling). Vipaka: Madhura (sweet post-digestive effect).
plants.medicalSignificance: Immunity booster, digestive, detox, anti-Pitta. It has cooling effect, thirst quencher, liver tonic, Pitta-balancing. It is rich in flavonoids (e.g. hesperidin, naringin) helps - Lower blood pressure, Reduce LDL cholesterol, Prevent atherosclerosis. Stimulate bile production, Improve digestion, Reduce nausea, bloating, and constipation. It boosts immunity, aids in collagen synthesis, helps in iron absorption, combats oxidative stress.

plants.name: Buddha's Hand Lemon
plants.vernacularName: Buddha's Hand Lemon / Buddha’s Hand Citron / Fingered Citron
plants.origin: India-China region. Northeastern India and China
plants.economicUse: Fruit is highly fragrant; used as a natural air freshener or perfume in homes and temples. The rind is rich in essential oils. It is used for culinary purposes: used for zest and flavoring in desserts, liqueurs (like citron liqueur), and savory dishes. Unlike most lemons, it has no juice or pulp, only rind and pith. Used as an offering in Buddhist temples, especially in China and Japan. It is comsidered as a symbol of happiness, longevity, and good fortune. Essential Oil estraction: Oil is extracted from the rind is used in perfumes, cosmetics, and aromatherapy.
plants.vedicSignificance:
It's parent specie — Citrus medica (Matulunga in Sanskrit) — is well documented. In Ayurveda, it's
Sanskrit name is Matulunga. Classified under: Deepana (appetizer), Pachana (digestive), Kaphahara (alleviates Kapha), Vatanulomana (carminative, supports proper Vata flow).
plants.medicalSignificance: It is an Antioxidant: Contains compounds that reduce oxidative stress. Anti-inflammatory: Used in treating inflammation-related conditions. Antispasmodic: Eases muscle spasms and gastrointestinal discomfort. Carminative: Helps relieve gas and bloating. Antimicrobial: Active against some bacteria and fungi. Analgesic: Mild pain relief properties. Respiratory Aid: Used in traditional medicine for cough, asthma, and congestion.

plants.name: Black mango
plants.origin: Indo-Mayanmar region. Northeastern India, Bangladesh, and the Myanmar region
plants.economicUse: Eaten fresh or processed (juice, pickles, chutneys). Exported for specialty fruit markets. Used in desserts and traditional sweets. Dried or powdered for spice blends (amchur).
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in Vitamin-A, C, E, and polyphenols. Antioxidant, boosts immunity, improves digestion. Leaves are used in traditional medicine for diabetes, respiratory issues, and wound healing. Bark and Seeds are used as astringent, used for diarrhea and dysentery.

plants.name: Peanut
plants.origin: South America, specifically the region around Southern Bolivia, Northern Argentina, and Paraguay
plants.economicUse:
Used as an oilseed crop for cooking and frying popular in Indian and African cuisine. Consumed raw Consumed raw, roasted, or boiled. Used in making peanut butter, snacks, confectionery, and flour. The press cake after oil extraction is high in protein and used as livestock feed
Used in soil enrichment: As a legume, it fixes nitrogen, improving soil fertility.
plants.vedicSignificance:
Mentioned in Ayurveda and nighantus (glossaries) for:
Balya (strength-promoting). Brimhana (bulk-promoting, nourishing). Vata-pacifying (due to its oiliness).
plants.medicalSignificance: Used to improve heart health, antioxidant, antidiabetic, cognitive support. It is Rich in: Protein, healthy fats (oleic acid), Vitamin E, B vitamins, folate, magnesium. Cardioprotective: Lowers LDL cholesterol; heart-friendly. Antioxidant: Contains resveratrol (same compound in red wine). Antidiabetic: Helps regulate blood sugar levels (low glycemic index). Anti-aging & skin health: Vitamin E and polyphenols promote skin regeneration. Brain health: Niacin and folate support cognitive function.

plants.name: Red Water Apple
plants.vernacularName: Red Water Apple / Rose Apple / Jambu /Bell Fruit / Java Apple
plants.origin: Native to: Malay Peninsula, Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Malaysia, and Indonesia
plants.economicUse: Used for fresh Consumption: Eaten raw as a juicy, mildly sweet fruit. Pickles & Preserves: Used in chutneys, jams, and traditional pickles. Ornamental Use: Grown as an ornamental tree in gardens due to its attractive foliage and fruit. Agroforestry: Used in home gardens and mixed plantations. Timber: Wood is sometimes used for light construction and firewood.
plants.vedicSignificance: Not mentioned in Ayurveda but used in folk medicine in Kerala, Tamil Nadu, and tribal systems (Siddha, Unani, and local traditions).
plants.medicalSignificance: It has polyphenols, flavonoids, tannins, and essential oils. Traditionally used in lowering blood sugar, reducing inflammation, managing diarrhea, treating sore throats and wounds.

plants.name: Thailand Mango
plants.vernacularName: Thailand Mango / Nam Dok Mai / Keo Savoy / Rad / Ok Rong /Chok Anan
plants.origin: Northeastern India, Myanmar, and Bangladesh
plants.economicUse: Fresh Consumption: High-quality dessert mangoes, often eaten ripe or slightly green. Export Crop: Major export item for Thailand, especially to Japan, Europe, and the Middle East. Desserts: Widely used in Thai dishes like mango sticky rice (Khao Niew Mamuang). Processed Products: Mango puree, juice, dried mango slices, ice creams. Agrotourism: Mango orchards are part of Thailand's rural tourism economy.
plants.vedicSignificance: Mentioned in Charaka Samhita and Sushruta Samhita. Mango is described as Vata-pacifying, Pitta-pacifying (when ripe), Brimhana (nourishing), Rasayana (rejuvenating).
plants.medicalSignificance: It gived cooling effect, it has digestive properties. It has antioxidant, promotes immunity. It has astringent, appetite stimulant, used in diarrhea. It is anti-diabetic, antioxidant, used in herbal teas. It is an astringent, used in traditional remedies for wounds, diarrhea.

plants.name: Rose
plants.origin: Asia (esp. China, Persia, India)
plants.economicUse: It is used as an ornamental plant in gardens, landscaping. It is used in perfumery as essential oils and in cosmetic industry. Used for culinary puroses rosewater, gulkand and sweets.
plants.vedicSignificance: Mentioned in Ayurveda/Vedic Literature known as “Shatapatrika” or “Taruni” in Ayurveda for balancing Pitta dosha.
plants.medicalSignificance: It is a mild laxative, it is anti-inflammatory. It is used for skin health and to cool the body. Rose petals used in preparations like gulkand for digestive aid.

plants.name: Pound Apple
plants.origin: Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia
plants.economicUse: Eaten fresh or made into chutneys, jams, jellies, and sherbets. Pulp is fermented into beverages. Tree wood used for tools. Fruit shells used as containers or decorative crafts.
plants.vedicSignificance:
In Ayurveda it ia known as Kapittha (कपित्थ) in Sanskrit. One of the Dashamoola (group of 10 roots used in Ayurvedic formulations). Considered sacred and associated with Lord Shiva. Ayurvedic Properties:
Rasa (taste): Astringent, sour, Virya: Ushna (hot potency), Vipaka: Katu (pungent), Dosha effects: Balances Vata and Kapha.
plants.medicalSignificance: It gives digestive aid – used to treat diarrhea, dysentery. It has antimicrobial – pulp and juice have antibacterial properties. It is anti-inflammatory – used for joint pain and swelling. It is rich in antioxidants, vitamin C, and fiber.

plants.name: Sapota
plants.origin: Southern Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean
plants.economicUse: It is grown for its sweet, pulpy fruit, consumed fresh or used in milkshakes, smoothies, desserts. It's latex (chicle) once used in chewing gum. It's wood is used in carpentry.
plants.vedicSignificance: In Ayurveda, it is known as Madhuphala or sometimes just Sapota. While not native to India, it has been incorporated into Unani and modern Ayurvedic practices. It is known for nourishing, cooling, and strengthening properties. Ayurvedic properties: Rasa: Madhura (sweet), Virya: Sheeta (cooling), Dosha: Pacifies Pitta and Vata.
plants.medicalSignificance: It is rich in dietary fiber – aids digestion and relieves constipation. It is a natural energy booster – high in fructose and sucrose. It contains vitamin A, C, iron, calcium, and antioxidants. It has mild sedative properties – sometimes used to ease stress.

plants.name: Phalsa Fruit
plants.origin: Tropical Asia & Africa
plants.economicUse: Fruit is edible, sour to sweet when ripe, often eaten fresh or made into jams, pickles, or fermented drinks. Bark and roots used in traditional medicine. Sometimes cultivated as a hedge plant due to its thorny branches.
plants.medicalSignificance: In traditional medicine, bark decoction used for diarrhea, dysentery, and sore throat. Fruit juice used as a mild laxative, leaves used externally for skin infections. In modern medicine, polyphenolics and anti-oxidants. It has anti-microbial and anti-inflamamtory properties.

plants.name: White Java Plum
plants.origin: Indian Subcontinent & Southeast Asia
plants.economicUse: Eaten fresh or made into juice, vinegar, wine, or pickles. Increasing market value due to rarity and medicinal demand. Used in herbal and natural remedies (seeds, bark, fruit).
plants.vedicSignificance: In Ayurveda: Known as Jambu, with white variety called Shweta Jambu. Considered highly beneficial for digestive issues and diabetes. Described in Charaka Samhita, Sushruta Samhita, and other classical texts. Ayurevdic properties: Rasa: Kashaya (astringent), Madhura (sweet), Virya: Sheeta (cooling), Dosha: Pacifies Pitta and Kapha.
plants.medicalSignificance: It is anti-diabetic: Helps regulate blood sugar levels (especially seed powder). It is an astringent: Useful in managing diarrhea, dysentery. It is antioxidant-rich: Strengthens immunity and protects cells. It has low glycemic index: Suitable for diabetic diets. Iyt improves skin and oral health (used in mouth rinses and pastes).

plants.name: Green Water Apple
plants.vernacularName: Green Water Apple / watery rose apple / Bell fruit / Jambu air (Malay) / Chomphu (Thai)
plants.origin: Southeast Asia, particularly Malaysia, Indonesia, The Andaman & Nicobar Islands
plants.economicUse: Fruit Consumption: Eaten fresh or in fruit salads, Used in pickles, jams, and juices. Agroforestry: Grown in home gardens; valued for shade and ornamental beauty. Local Trade: Common in local markets in tropical countries. Minor export product in some Southeast Asian countries.
plants.medicalSignificance: It has antioxidant properties. Anti-inflammatory and antibacterial effects. Potential anti-diabetic effects (less studied than S. cumini)

plants.name: Snake Fruit
plants.vernacularName: Snake Fruit / Salak / Salacca / Snake fruit
plants.origin: Indonesia, particularly Java and Sumatra
plants.economicUse: Eaten fresh as a sweet and tangy snack. Used in desserts, pickles, and local delicacies. Processed Products: Used in making jams, juices, chips, and fermented beverages. A delicacy in Southeast Asian markets. Featured in agrotourism and tropical fruit festivals.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in dietary fiber – aids digestion. Contains potassium, iron, vitamin C. Known to improve eye health due to beta-carotene content. Traditionally used in teas and treating diarrhea. Has antioxidant and antimicrobial properties. It is anti-diabetic potential: May help regulate blood glucose. Has anti-obesity: Promotes satiety due to high fiber content

plants.name: Duku
plants.origin: Malaysia and Indonesia particularly Java & Sumatra
plants.economicUse: Fruits are sweet, juicy, and slightly tangy eaten raw or used in tropical fruit salads. Made into syrups, jams, and preserves. Seeds used for local medicinal products. Wood sometimes used for light construction or fuel
plants.medicalSignificance: It has antioxidant Properties: High in polyphenols and flavonoids. It is anti-malarial Potential: Bark extracts show promise in early studies. It is antimicrobial and antifungal. Helpful in wound Healing & anti-inflammatory: Observed in some animal models

plants.name: Pista
plants.origin: Western Asia and the Middle East
plants.economicUse: Consumed as dried nut, raw, roasted, or salted. Used in ice creams, halwa, baklava, kulfi, sweets, and savory dishes. Pistachio oil used in gourmet and cosmetic applications. High-value export crop, especially from Iran and the US
plants.vedicSignificance:
Mentioned in Ayurveda, though not native to India, under names like Pista and sometimes as Vatad (general nut category)

Valued as: Balya (strength-giving), Vrishya (aphrodisiac), Medhya (brain tonic)
plants.medicalSignificance: Cardioprotective: Regular consumption improves HDL, lowers LDL. Anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects. Supports gut microbiota due to high fiber content. May improve sexual health and sperm quality. May reduce oxidative stress in metabolic syndrome

plants.name: Zamiya Kulkas
plants.vernacularName: Zamiya Kulkas / ZZ Plant / Zanzibar Gem, Zuzu plant, Emerald Palm
plants.origin: Eastern Africa particularly Kenya,Tanzania, Zanzibar, Malawi
plants.economicUse: Widely used in indoor decoration for homes, offices. Thrives in low-light environments; popular for urban settings. Nursery plant with high demand in the houseplant market. Propagated easily by division or leaf cuttings
plants.medicalSignificance: Toxic to humans and pets

plants.name: Lakshman Phala
plants.origin: Tropical Americas and the Caribbean
plants.economicUse: Fresh fruit is consumed as juice, smoothies, ice creams, jams, and syrups. White pulp is fibrous, aromatic, and mildly acidic. Used in health supplements (especially in Latin America). Tea from leaves sold as herbal remedy (though caution is advised). Grown in home gardens and small organic farms in tropical climates
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in vitamin C, fiber, and potassium. Boosts immunity, supports digestion, and hydrates. Used to relieve fever and intestinal parasites.Used as a tea or poultice for inflammation, joint pain, sleep disorders, and high BP. Claimed to have anticancer properties. Traditionally used externally for lice and skin disorders

plants.name: Red Cherry
plants.vernacularName: Red Cherry / Tart Cherry, Bird Cherry
plants.origin: Europe and Western Asia. Sour cherry (Prunus cerasus): Native to Europe and Southwest Asia
plants.economicUse: Edible Fruit is consumed fresh, dried, or processed into juices, jams, sauces, and desserts. Used in baking (pies, tarts) and beverages (liqueurs, wines). Cherry trees are valued for their beautiful spring blossoms (especially ornamental cherry blossoms). Cherry wood is prized in furniture making for its color and grain
plants.medicalSignificance: Anthocyanins in cherries have potent anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects. Clinical studies suggest benefits for osteoarthritis and gout symptom relief. Melatonin content supports improved sleep quality.Cherry consumption may help reduce blood pressure and improve vascular function

plants.name: Egg fruit
plants.origin: Southern Mexico - Central America (Guatemala, Belize, El Salvador)
plants.economicUse: Consumed fresh, or blended into smoothies, milkshakes, and desserts. Used as a vegan alternative to egg yolk in baking due to its texture. Sometimes made into flour or puree. Rich in carotenoids, niacin, and fiber. High-energy food in local diets
plants.medicalSignificance: Consumed fresh, or blended into smoothies, milkshakes, and desserts. Used as a vegan alternative to egg yolk in baking due to its texture. Sometimes made into flour or puree. Rich in carotenoids, niacin, and fiber. High-energy food in local diets. Grown in orchards or home gardens in tropical/subtropical zones

plants.name: Currant Berry
plants.vernacularName: Currant Berry / European Currant / Blackcurrant / Redcurrant
plants.botanicalName:
Ribes rubrum – Red currant
Ribes nigrum – Black currant
plants.origin: Europe and Northern Asia
plants.economicUse: Eaten fresh, dried, or processed into jams, jellies, sauces, juices, icecreames and liqueurs. Widely used in desserts and confectionery. Currant extracts are used in vitamin C supplements, eye health tonics, and anti-inflammatory products. Black currant seed oil used in skin care for its high gamma-linolenic acid (GLA) content
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in vitamin C, anthocyanins, and gamma-linolenic acid. Supports immune health, eye health, and joint function. Shows anti-inflammatory, anti-viral, and cardio-protective properties. Lower in vitamin C than black currant. Used as a gentle digestive tonic and cooling fruit in summer. Used in European folk medicine as diuretic, gout relief, and arthritis remedy

plants.name: Anjira
plants.origin: Western Asia and the Mediterranean region
plants.economicUse: Consumed fresh or dried. Used in sweets, jams, baked goods, and health foods. Dried figs are a valuable export commodity. Used as a natural laxative, blood purifier, and rejuvenator in traditional medicine. Grown in orchards and home gardens in semi-arid regions
plants.vedicSignificance: Known in Ayurveda as "Anjeera" / "Phalgu". Used in various Rasayana (rejuvenation) therapies. Mentioned in Charaka Samhita and other texts for: Balya (strength-giving), Vrishya (aphrodisiac), Anulomana (improves digestion and elimination)
plants.medicalSignificance: Contains antioxidants, flavonoids, and polyphenols. Shown to have hypoglycemic (blood sugar-lowering) properties. It is antibacterial, anti-inflammatory, and anticancer potential (early studies). Supportive for heart health and digestive regulation

plants.name: Silver Berry
plants.vernacularName: Silver Berry / Russian Olive / Oleaster / Wild Olive / Trepang Fruit
plants.origin: Central Asia, Southern Europe, and Western China
plants.economicUse: Small, oval, silvery-yellow fruits eaten raw or dried. Used in local desserts and jams. Fruits are nutritious and high in sugars. Widely used in Persian, Unani, and Central Asian medicine. Popular in Iranian herbal tonics and anti-inflammatory remedies. Used for soil stabilization, windbreaks, and ornamental planting
plants.medicalSignificance: Contains flavonoids, tannins, and linoleic acid. It's clinical studies (especially in Iran) show: Pain relief in osteoarthritis. Antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. Potential neuroprotective effects. Used in traditional Persian sports medicine to improve recovery and joint strength

plants.name: Karpura
plants.origin: China, Japan, Taiwan (East Asia)
plants.economicUse:
Used in religious practices - Burned in Hindu pujas, aarti, and temples. Symbolizes purity and dispels negativity. Medicinal Use: Used in Ayurveda, Siddha, and Unani systems. Present in balms, oils, ointments for cough, cold, joint pain.
Source of camphor oil used in perfumery, aromatherapy, and pharmaceuticals
plants.vedicSignificance: Widely mentioned in classical Ayurvedic texts like Charaka Samhita, Sushruta Samhita, and Ashtanga Hridayam. It is recognized for: Shwasahara (relieves breathing difficulty). Shothahara (anti-inflammatory). Kusthaghna (treats skin diseases). Grahi (absorbs excess moisture). Also known as Bhimseni Karpura (natural camphor)
plants.medicalSignificance: Active compound: Cineole, borneol, camphene. It shows anti-inflammatory, antibacterial, antifungal effects, neurostimulant action (increases alertness, clears mind), effective in topical pain relief

plants.name: Pulasan
plants.origin: Peninsular Malaysia, Borneo, and Philippines
plants.economicUse: The white translucent aril (flesh) is sweet, aromatic, and non-acidic. Consumed fresh, or used in juices, desserts, and jams. Pulasan tree wood is sometimes used in tool handles and furniture. Grown in home gardens and small orchards
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in phenolics and antioxidants. It shows potential for anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial activity. Anti-aging and immune-boosting effects (early studies)

plants.name: Wood Apple
plants.origin: Indian subcontinent — India, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh
plants.economicUse: Edible Fruit: Pulp is used in chutneys, sherbets, jams, and juices. High in pectin – useful in making jellies and marmalades. Medicinal Use: Fruit pulp, leaves, bark, and root are all used in Ayurveda and folk medicine. Cultural Use: Often offered in temples, especially in South India. Used in traditional medicine markets
plants.vedicSignificance: Mentioned in Ayurvedic literature under names like: Kapith, Dadhittha, Kapittha. Different from Bael/Aegle marmelos, but sometimes associated. Ayurvedic Properties: Rasa (Taste): Kashaya (astringent), Madhura (sweet), Virya (Potency): Ushna (hot), Vipaka: Katu (pungent), Dosha: Balances Kapha and Vata, slightly aggravates Pitta
plants.medicalSignificance: It is antidiarrheal – treats dysentery, diarrhea. Appetizer – stimulates digestion. Relieves constipation, bloating, and flatulence. Leaves are used for liver ailments and blood purification. Roots and Bark: Ground into pastes or decoctions for fever, infections, and wound healing

plants.name: Violet Apple
plants.vernacularName: Violet Apple / Star Apple / Cainito / Milk Fruit
plants.origin: Caribbean and Central America (e.g., Panama, Dominican Republic)
plants.economicUse:
Edible Fruit: The translucent-white to purple pulp is sweet and eaten fresh. Used in desserts, smoothies, salads, and ice creams
Shade Tree / Ornamental Use: Planted for its glossy foliage and beautiful purple fruit. Popular in tropical home gardens. Wood Use: Wood is hard and durable, used locally for construction and furniture
plants.medicalSignificance: Fruit pulp is rich in vitamin C, calcium, and antioxidants. Helps cool the body, and soothes gastritis and ulcers. Mild laxative effect – relieves constipation. Leaves are used in decoctions for diabetes, inflammation, and hypertension. Bark is traditionally used for dysentery and diarrhea

plants.name: Apple Berry Red
plants.vernacularName:
Apple Berry Red / Apple Dumpling (Australia) /
Bush Tucker Berr
plants.origin: Australia – particularly New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland, and South Australia
plants.economicUse: Edible Fruit is consumed raw when fully ripe (has an apple/kiwi-like taste). Used in bush tucker cuisine, jams, chutneys, and sauces. Used in landscaping popular in native Australian gardens as a ground cover or climber. I is a good wildlife plant and attracts birds and native bees
plants.medicalSignificance: Fruits are traditionally used by Aboriginal Australians. Mild nutrient-rich fruit – source of vitamin C and antioxidants. Leaves/Bark are anti-inflammatory

plants.name: Orange Jasmine
plants.vernacularName: Orange Jasmine / Mock Orange/ Maddu Kamini / Kunti
plants.origin: South and Southeast Asia – India, Sri Lanka, southern China, Malaysia, and the Philippines
plants.economicUse: It is a popular hedge plant, especially in gardens and public landscaping. Grown for its highly fragrant white flowers. Flowers used in local perfumes and oils. Extracts are used in natural cosmetics. Used in Ayurvedic, Unani, and folk medicine systems
plants.vedicSignificance:
Ayurvedic or Vedic Mentions
Referred to in Ayurveda as "Kunti" Flowers and leaves used in formulations for: Vata disorders, Digestive problems, Skin issues
plants.medicalSignificance: Leave are used to treat fever, headache, and digestive disorders. Infusions used for cough, cold, and body aches. Flowers are mild sedative and fragrance therapy. Used for aromatherapy and mental calmness. Bark & roots are occasionally used in treating dysentery, rheumatism, and intestinal worms

plants.name: Chayamanza
plants.vernacularName: Chayamanza / Chaya / Tree Spinach / Mayan Spinach
plants.origin: Central America, particularly the Yucatán Peninsula (Mexico)
plants.economicUse:
Leaves and tender shoots are cooked and eaten like spinach. They must be thoroughly boiled to neutralize toxic cyanide compounds. 
Nutrient-dense food: High in protein, vitamins (A, B, C), calcium, iron, and antioxidants
plants.medicalSignificance: Hypocholesterolemic: Reduced cholesterol by ~28–31% in animal models. It is an antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, cardioprotective effects observed in lab and animal studies. Nutritional profiling: protein ~32–34 g/100 g dry, high phenolic content; cooking removes harmful cyanides significantly. Proposed benefits include hepatoprotective, antidiabetic, and neuroprotective effects.

plants.name: Arpina Hannu
plants.origin: Peninsular India—including Western Ghats and Eastern Ghats region
plants.economicUse: Produces small edible fruits (yellow to orange), consumed raw, jammed. Seasonal jams and preserves made from wild-harvested fruit, used in local cuisine and home store.
plants.medicalSignificance: Not documented

plants.name: Terminalia
plants.botanicalName: Terminalia chebula (Haritaki), Terminalia bellirica (Bibhitaki), Terminalia arjuna (Arjuna), Terminalia cattapa (Indian almond)
plants.origin:
Tropical and subtropical regions:

South and Southeast Asia (India, Sri Lanka, Himalayas)
plants.economicUse:
Used extensively in Ayurvedic, Unani, Tibetan, Chinese, and African traditional medicines for their health benefits. Formulation Ingredients:
Core ingredients in Triphala (chebula, bellirica, and emblica), a widely used Ayurvedic rasayana. Non-medicinal Uses:
