Some species, like T. catappa, are grown as ornamental shade trees, or harvested for tannins, resins, and wood for tools/furniture
plants.vedicSignificance:
Abundantly mentioned in Ayurveda. 1. T. chebula (Haritaki): Called the “King of Medicines” in Ayurveda, extensively described in classical texts for broad-spectrum rejuvenation and digestive health. 2. T. bellirica (Bibhitaki): Sanskrit name Bibhitaka or Behada, used in Triphala; described in Charaka Samhita for respiratory and throat conditions, digestive cleansing, and longevity. 
3. T. arjuna: Used traditionally for cardiovascular health, heart disease, dysentery, urinary issues, and scorpion bites; well documented in Ayurvedic texts and folk medicine. 4. T. cattapa: Used for skin, fever, liver conditions, anti-diabetic, anti-bacterial, anti-HIV activity in some regions.
plants.medicalSignificance:
Antioxidant & anti-inflammatory (lowers oxidative stress). Antimicrobial (bacterial, fungal, antiviral, antimycobacterial). Antidiabetic / hypoglycemic (e.g. chebulagic acid inhibits α‑glucosidase. Cardioprotective / liver protective, especially T. arjuna bark extracts in trials.
Anti‑cancer and cytotoxic effects in early-stage studies. Hair-growth benefits from T. bellirica extracts compared to finasteride in animal/in vitro models

plants.name: Sweet Red Mooty
plants.vernacularName: Sweet Red Mooty / Mooty fruit or Mooti Pazham
plants.origin: Western Ghats of Peninsular India, especially Kerala (Pathanamthitta, Wayanad)
plants.economicUse: Fresh fruits are consumed locally; tastes sweet with mild sour or bitter notes depending on color (red sweeter, yellow or rose tone more bitter). Outer husk used to make pickles, inner pulp used in drink, jam, and preserve making.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in vitamin C, polyphenols, flavonoids, potassium, calcium, magnesium; provides dietary fiber and antioxidants. Supports immune health. Manages blood pressure and cholesterol. Helps digestive regulation and prevents constipation. May show anti-inflammatory and anticancer potential in preliminary studies

plants.name: Keledang
plants.origin: Southeast Asia—found in the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, and Borneo
plants.economicUse: Fruits are round (8–12 cm dia) with thick rough skin in reddish-orange tones. Inside are pods of yellow‑orange aril around dark seeds. The pulp is sweet, aromatic, and similar in taste to a mix of jackfruit and mangosteen. Seeds are sometimes roasted and eaten. Trees produce beautiful wood used for furniture or fittings in local settings.
plants.medicalSignificance: Fruits are believed to support digestion, immunity, and skin health due to antioxidant-rich pulp. Seeds are roasted and consumed; little medicinal use documented. Bark/Leaves are traditionally used reported beyond general tonic use in native contexts.

plants.name: Achachairu
plants.origin: Bolivian Amazon basin—especially the Santa Cruz and Porongo regions
plants.economicUse: Eaten fresh and used in ice creams, juices, sorbets, jams, and cocktails. Peel is used to make tart beverages—boiled or blended with sugar and water as a refreshing drink. Edible after soaking and roasting, often used as snack or added to dishes
plants.medicalSignificance:
Eaten fresh considered refreshing, hydrating, and a light digestive tonic; used traditionally in Amazon region for inflammation, weight control, and soothing skin/gastrointestinal ailments.
Peel (Rind)	Employed in Amazonian folk medicine as an appetite suppressant, and often used in thirst-quenching drinks considered detoxifying. Occasionally consumed after preparation; used in traditional settings for mild nutrition; no major therapeutic use documented.

plants.name: Malabar Chestnut
plants.vernacularName: Malabar Chestnut / Money Tree Nut / Saba Nut / Guiana Chestnut / Provision Tree / French Peanut
plants.origin: Central and South American wetlands and lowland rainforests, ranging from Mexico through northern Brazil
plants.economicUse:
Seeds (nuts) are edible raw or roasted, with a taste similar to peanuts or chestnuts. They can be ground into flour or used in baked goods and as a snack.
Young leaves and flower buds are edible when cooked and used as a leafy vegetable in stir-fries, soups, and salads.
Widely grown as a decorative plant; indoor “braided trunk” versions are popular gifts believed to bring good luck (“money tree”).
Valued for its large palmate leaves, showy fragrant flowers, and adaptability to indoor/outdoor settings
plants.medicalSignificance: Applied in traditional herbal medicine for hepatitis. Used as infusion for headaches, anemia, stomach discomfort, blood tonic and mild diuretic. Leaves (infusion)	Employed topically or internally for skin irritation, burning sensations, and as a mild health tonic.

plants.name: Guava Japan Red
plants.vernacularName: Guava Japan Red / Red Diamond Guava
plants.origin: Central and South America
plants.economicUse: Large fruit, typically 400–1,000 g each. Almost seedless (5–10 small seeds). Sweet, aromatic, with reddish-pink flesh ideal for fresh eating, juices, jam, and Compact growth habit suitable for pots or small gardens. Fruits 2–3 times per year in favorable climates
plants.vedicSignificance: Guava is well-regarded in Ayurveda for its digestive support, anti‑diarrheal, and antimicrobial benefits.  Used in folk medicine for headache, cough, gum disease, and diarrhea
plants.medicalSignificance: Fruit pulp is high in vitamin C, fiber, and antioxidants — supports immunity, digestive health, and heart function. Leaves (general guava) are used in traditional remedies for diarrhea, cough, oral ulcers, anti-inflammatory, antibacterial activity.

plants.name: Manila Tennis Ball Cherry
plants.vernacularName: Manila Tennis Ball Cherry / Manila Cherry /
plants.origin: Tropical regions—probably Southeast Asia / India
plants.economicUse: Grown as a fruit tree or ornamental shrub, often grafted for fruit production. Produces round, red tennis-ball-sized fruits—tangy-sweet, used fresh or in jams, juices, desserts, and eaten raw in tropical regions. Also valued for landscaping and hedges due to dense foliage and manageable size
plants.medicalSignificance: Antioxidant‑rich fruit, believed to boost immunity and reduce oxidative stress. Traditional use in managing diarrhoea, digestive disorders, asthma and respiratory ailments. Anaemia (possibly due to iron content). Blood sugar regulation (used for diabetes).

plants.name: Lemon
plants.origin: Northeastern India, Northern Myanmar, and China
plants.economicUse: Commercially grown for fresh fruits, juice extraction, pickles, and culinary use. Lemon oil (from peel) used in perfumery, cosmetics, and cleaning products. Lemon peel and seeds are also used in traditional medicine and food processing.
plants.vedicSignificance: Mentioned in Ayurveda as “Nimbuka” or “Jambira” in Ayurvedic texts. Reference in Charaka Samhita, Sushruta Samhita. Used traditionally to balance Kapha and Vata doshas.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in Vitamin C – boosts immunity and acts as an antioxidant. Aids digestion, helps in detoxification, and reduces acidity. Antibacterial and antifungal properties. Juice used for treating sore throat, nausea, and scurvy. Promoting skin clarity and weight management. Peel extracts also have anti-inflammatory and cholesterol-lowering effects.

plants.name: Santol Sweet Santol
plants.vernacularName: Santol Sweet Santol / Cotton Fruit / Lolly Fruit / Sentul
plants.origin: Indochina and Peninsular Malaysia
plants.economicUse: Grown as a fruit-bearing ornamental tree in home gardens or for shade in urban areas. Produces large fruits with thick leathery rind and cotton-like edible pulp. Inner segments are juicy, translucent-white, with sweet‑sour flavor. Eaten fresh and used in making jams, chutneys, preserves, pickles, sauces, and curries due to its sour taste
plants.medicalSignificance: Digestive aid: fiber-rich flesh supports digestion and regularity. Immune booster: rich in antioxidants and vitamin C. Cardiometabolic support: may help reduce LDL cholesterol and aid weight control. Other folkloric uses: treatment of diarrhea, constipation, leucorrhea, anemia, hemorrhoids, inflammation, anti-aging, anti-allergy, and even as a natural insect repellent in some cultures.

plants.name: Mango variety Priyoor
plants.origin: Piyoor variety of mango originated from Kerala
plants.economicUse: Fruit characterized by oblong shape; smooth green‑yellow rind; fiberless, sweet juicy flesh. Premium fruit for fresh eating and juices and export
plants.vedicSignificance: Mentioned in Ayurveda. Unripe form may aggravate Pitta/Kapha/Vata depending on constitution
plants.medicalSignificance: Mango demonstrates antioxidant, anti‑inflammatory, antiviral, hypotensive, cardiotonic, immunomodulatory, antimicrobial, and hepatoprotective effects, among others. Additional activities include antidiabetic, antipyretic, antidiarrhoeal, antiparasitic, antitumor, hypolipidemic, antiallergic, and gastroprotective properties.

plants.name: Mango variety Black Rose
plants.origin: Southern India, especially Kerala and Karnataka
plants.economicUse: Fruit characterized by large size, purple‑black skin, fiberless sweet flesh. Positioned as a premium fruit for fresh eating, favored in local markets and potentially boutique export/culinary use
plants.vedicSignificance: Mentioned in Ayurveda. Unripe form may aggravate Pitta/Kapha/Vata depending on constitution
plants.medicalSignificance: Mango demonstrates antioxidant, anti‑inflammatory, antiviral, hypotensive, cardiotonic, immunomodulatory, antimicrobial, and hepatoprotective effects, among others. Additional activities include antidiabetic, antipyretic, antidiarrhoeal, antiparasitic, antitumor, hypolipidemic, antiallergic, and gastroprotective properties.

plants.name: Bush Orange
plants.origin: Unspecific
plants.economicUse: Grown for small‐fruit yield and compact garden use.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in vitamin C, dietary fiber, and antioxidants; supports heart and brain health.

plants.name: Arazaboi
plants.origin: Western Amazon region—Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador
plants.economicUse:
Eaten fresh. Pale green to bright yellow when ripe; very acidic pulp with juicy, aromatic flavor.
Culinary uses: Typically too sour to eat fresh raw—commonly used in juices, nectar, marmalade, ice creams, jams, squash, and smoothies.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in vitamins & nutrients: Extremely high vitamin C, notable vitamin A, B1, fiber, proteins, potassium, and antioxidants like terpenes and volatile compounds—suggested roles in supporting digestion, bowel health, blood pressure control, cancer prevention

plants.name: West Indian Cherry
plants.origin: South America, Central America, and the Caribbean especially the West Indies
plants.economicUse: Widely grown for its small, bright red, cherry-like fruit. Consumed fresh or processed into juices, jams, and vitamin C supplements. Major source of natural vitamin C (ascorbic acid)—about 30–50 times more than oranges. Used in dietary supplements and health tonics. Used in skin care products for its antioxidant
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in Vitamin C: Boosts immunity. Supports collagen formation. Improves iron absorption. Antioxidant Properties: Protects against oxidative stress and inflammation. Antimicrobial and Antifungal: Traditionally used to treat coughs, colds, and diarrhea. Liver Health: Shows hepatoprotective effects in traditional medicine. It supports skin health.

plants.name: Cedar Bay Cherry
plants.origin: Northern Queensland (Australia), Indonesia, and some parts of Pacific Islands
plants.economicUse: Eaten fresh as sweet taste. It is used in jams, jellies, and sauces in local and niche gourmet markets. Popular as a landscaping shrub or small tree in tropical gardens due to its attractive foliage and bright fruit. Fruit is a food source for birds and other wildlife in its native habitat.
plants.medicalSignificance: The fruit contains antioxidants, which may support immune function and reduce oxidative stress. Indigenous Australian communities have traditionally consumed the fruit as bush tucker (native food). Leaves and bark sometimes used in folk remedies for skin irritations and infections. Early studies suggest potential anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial properties.

plants.name: Bignay
plants.origin: Southeast Asia, especially the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia
plants.economicUse: Fruits are eaten fresh or processed into jams, wines, juices, and vinegar. Bignay wine is particularly popular in the Philippines. Used as a shade/ornamental tree in tropical gardens and farms. Agroforestry and Reforestation: Valued in reforestation projects due to its fast growth and resilience.
plants.medicalSignificance: Cardiovascular Health: Contains anthocyanins and flavonoids that may help reduce blood pressure and cholesterol. Rich in polyphenols that help combat oxidative stress and inflammation. It has antidiabetic potential, traditionally used in managing blood sugar levels. Antimicrobial Activity: Leaves and bark used in folk medicine for wound healing, treating ulcers, and skin infections.

plants.name: Matoa
plants.vernacularName: Matoa /  Fijian Longan / Island Lychee / Kasai/ Oceanic Lychee
plants.origin: Papua New Guinea, Indonesia, and parts of Southeast Asia and the Pacific Islands.
plants.economicUse: Eaten fresh. Timber Use: The wood is strong and durable; used in construction, furniture, and carving. Agroforestry: Grown in mixed-crop systems and home gardens in tropical regions. Local Markets: An important fruit in Indonesian local economies, especially in eastern provinces.
plants.medicalSignificance: Antioxidant-rich: The fruit is high in polyphenols and flavonoids that may help combat free radicals. Anti-inflammatory: Traditional uses include reducing inflammation and promoting skin healing. Supports Immunity: Vitamin C content supports immune health. Antimicrobial Potential: Bark and leaves used in traditional medicine for their antibacterial and antifungal properties. Digestive Health: Traditionally used to relieve constipation and indigestion. Scientific research is still emerging on Matoa’s medicinal properties, with some pharmacological interest in its antioxidant and antimicrobial effects.

plants.name: Kepal
plants.origin: Java and broader Malesia region (Indonesia, Malaysia)
plants.economicUse: Edible fruits which are sweet, orange like pulp. Grown as an elegant ornamental tree for its glossy foliage and cauliflorous fruiting. Wood was occasionally utilized for durable household items.
plants.medicalSignificance: Bioactive Constituents: Fruit flesh, seeds, and roots contain saponins, flavonoids, polyphenols, and alkaloids; also vitamins C and A, terpenes, and quercetin among others. Liver Protection (Hepatoprotective): Studies indicate the fruit pulp supports liver enzyme function and aids cell regeneration. Natural Deodorant & Diuretic: Traditional use includes controlling body odor, improving urinary output, and reducing kidney inflammation. Gout & Anti‑Inflammatory: Alkaloid content helps manage joint pain and gout; terpenes and quercetin support cell repair and reduce inflammation. Anti‑cancer Potential: Compounds like acetogenins, styryl lactones, and isoflavones show preliminary anti-tumor effects in research contexts.

plants.name: Mango var. Chang Deang
plants.origin: Thailand, though also cultivated in India, the Philippines
plants.economicUse: Fruit characterized by large size, purple‑black skin, fiberless sweet flesh. Positioned as a premium fruit for fresh eating, favored in local markets and potentially boutique export/culinary use
plants.vedicSignificance: Mentioned in Ayurveda. Unripe form may aggravate Pitta/Kapha/Vata depending on constitution
plants.medicalSignificance: Mango demonstrates antioxidant, anti‑inflammatory, antiviral, hypotensive, cardiotonic, immunomodulatory, antimicrobial, and hepatoprotective effects, among others. Additional activities include antidiabetic, antipyretic, antidiarrhoeal, antiparasitic, antitumor, hypolipidemic, antiallergic, and gastroprotective properties.

plants.name: Sweet Ambazham
plants.vernacularName: Sweet Ambazham / Indian Hog Plum / Indian Hog
plants.origin: South and Southeast Asia, including India, Sri Lanka, and Indo‑Malaysia region
plants.economicUse: Sweet Ambazham is eaten fresh. Used pickled, juiced, or used in chutneys and desserts. Agroforestry: Medium-sized tree reaching up to ~25 m in the wild; compact grafted forms are used in gardens and containers. Often planted in India as fruiting trees; lesser-known in commercial export markets but valued locally and suited to home orchards
plants.vedicSignificance: n Ayurveda, the plant has kashaya, amla, madhura tastes; guru (heavy), snigdha (unctuous) quality; cooling virya. It is considered digestive, astringent, antiscorbutic, and useful for dysentery, dyspepsia, earache, stomach disorders, and biliousness
plants.medicalSignificance:
Rich in Vitamin C, flavonoids, phenolics, and tannins—the fruit is used traditionally as a refreshing and astringent tonic. Useful parts include leaf, bark, root, and fruit. 
Folk Uses: Bark and leaves used for diarrhea, dyspepsia, skin infections; root decoctions for menstrual regulation; leaf juice for earaches; fruit for digestive support. Anti-inflammatory & Astringent: Used traditionally to treat dysentery, gastro‑intestinal upsets, and rheumatism

plants.name: Apple var. Diamond Black
plants.origin: Mountains of Nyingchi, Tibet
plants.economicUse: Extremely rare, sold in upscale grocery stores as luxury/exotic fruit.
plants.medicalSignificance: Contains dietary fiber, vitamins A, B, C, and antioxidants. Some descriptions highlight sweetness, crispness, and unique flavor notes like honey, vanilla, almond after storage

plants.name: Longan var. Diamond River
plants.origin: Southeast Asia and Pacific Islands — native to Papua New Guinea, Indonesia, and parts of Melanesia
plants.economicUse: Eaten fresh for it's translucent pulp is sweet and juicy with a floral aroma. Grown in Kerala by exotic fruit nurseries.
plants.medicalSignificance:
Rich in vitamin C, small amounts of B vitamins, and fiber.
Traditional uses in Chinese herbal medicine: dried longan promotes relaxation, supports digestion, and is used in soups and tonics. Antioxidant polyphenols and mild glycemic effects typical of longan fruit

plants.name: Longkong
plants.origin: Southeast Asia—primarily Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines
plants.economicUse: Edible fruit is translucent, juicy, sweet-sour. Sold fresh in regional markets across Southeast Asia. Grown in home orchards and small farms; limited export availability due to perishability.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in vitamin A, B1 (thiamine), B2 (riboflavin), and C, along with minerals such as phosphorus, iron, potassium, and dietary fiber. Includes natural sugars like sucrose, fructose, glucose. Considered low in calories. Consumed fresh as a refreshing tonic; young fruit extracts are under study for antioxidant and possibly anti‑cancer bioactivity

plants.name: Kak Jam
plants.origin: Bangladesh, India, Myanmar, China, and Thailand.
plants.economicUse: Fruits are flavorful, subacid to astringent, commonly eaten fresh by local children in rural areas. Fodder and Fuel: leaves are used as fodder; wood used for fuel in local communities. Ornamental / Wildlife Use: Planted in gardens or margins to attract birds; valued for its foliage and fruit-bearing clusters.
plants.medicalSignificance: Leaf decoction: Used traditionally to treat anaemia. Leaf juice: Administered to relieve blood-dysentery and gastrointestinal complaints. Seeds: Suggested as a potential nutraceutical source for preventing chronic degenerative diseases (phytotherapy research)

plants.name: Rain Forest Plum
plants.vernacularName: Rain Forest Plum / Cambuí Roxo / Murtinha
plants.origin: Atlantic rainforest of Brazil, especially eastern Brazil
plants.economicUse: FEaten raw as fresh fruit. Used in fruit processing often processed into jams, jellies, ice creams, juices, and even used unpitted in baking for intense color and flavor. The tree’s bright green glossy foliage and seasonal flowers make it an attractive ornamental for gardens and patios, flowering and fruiting multiple times per year (4–6 cycles).
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in Nutrients: contains vitamin E, lutein (even more than avocado), and minerals like zinc, folate, calcium, potassium, and magnesium. Used in folk medicine in parts of Brazil (e.g., Sergipe), leaf infusions are traditionally used to relieve pain and fever. Leaf essential oil (~0.14% yield) contains sesquiterpenes such as guaiol, cadinol, δ‑elemene, and viridiflorene, contributing to its medicinal activity

plants.name: Mafai Mooty
plants.vernacularName: Mafai Mooty / Kafai Mooti / Burmese Grape
plants.origin: Southeast Asia—including Assam (India), Myanmar, Thailand, Peninsular Malaysia, Sumatra, Borneo, and Java
plants.economicUse: Eaten fresh as fruits with translucent pinkish pulp. Flavor ranges from sweet to sub-acid, often described as juicy and aromatic. Processed, stewed, pickled or fermented (often into local drinks or compotes). Ornamental & shade: It is an attractive medium-sized evergreen tree used in tropical gardens; also sold as grafted or seedling plants in nurseries in India and Southeast Asia.
plants.medicalSignificance: Likely contains vitamin C, minerals, dietary fiber, and natural sugars—akin to related species. Traditionally used as fruit for digestion; bark, seeds, or wood used in folk medicine for skin diseases and general health tonics (not widely documented). Bioactive potential: As other Baccaurea species are rich in polyphenols and anthocyanins, it may offer antioxidant and anti-inflammatory benefits (but direct studies on B. racemosa are scarce)

plants.name: Lubika Sweet
plants.vernacularName: Lubika Sweet / Sweet Lubikka / Sweet Lobi / Luvikka / Lovlolika
plants.origin: Tropical Asia, likely originating in India and Sri Lanka
plants.economicUse: Edible fruit is a berry, mildly sour-tangy in flavor. Consumed raw, or processed into jams, marmalades, chutneys, pickles, and occasionally used in curries or beverages. Grafted or seed-grown trees are sold in nurseries. Occasionally used for lumber/timber.
plants.medicalSignificance: Traditionally used for the bark has medicinal applications in folk medicine (especially in Kerala), and the fruits are used as digestive aids. Leaf and bark extracts may have astringent and tonic properties. Phytochemistry: Fruits and plant parts contain tannins. It may offer antioxidant and antimicrobial effects similar to related species.

plants.name: Strawberry var. Yellow Wonder
plants.vernacularName: Strawberry var. Yellow Wonder / Yellow Alpine Strawberry
plants.origin: Europe and parts of Asia, adapted to cool temperate zones.
plants.economicUse: Eaten fresh and raw, poduces small, creamy golden-yellow berries throughout the growing season with a sweet, aromatic flavour. Popular in home gardens; ideal for borders or landscaping, forms compact clumps (no runners).
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in Vitamin-C, fiber, and antioxidants. While cultivar-specific research is limited, Fragaria vesca generally supports antioxidant activity, digestive health, and has mild anti-inflammatory effects as known from herbal traditions.

plants.name: Terengganu Cherry
plants.origin: Southeast Asia, particularly Borneo, Philippines, Malaysia (Johore, Sabah, Sarawak) and parts of Indonesia
plants.economicUse: Edible freash and raw, produces glossy oval drupes. Fruits are highly prized fresh or in fruit salad and traditional desserts. An exotic ornamental plant, cultivated in tropical gardens for its attractive purple young foliage, pendulous flower clusters and vivid fruit assemblages used in landscaping.
plants.medicalSignificance: Ripe fruits contain 9.5% dietary fiber & Vitamin-C. Rich in polyphenols and anthocyanins - epicatechin as key catechin compound; seed and peel extracts showed DPPH radical scavenging activities of up to ~93% in ethanol extract. Antidiabetic Potential: Leaf extracts, particularly proanthocyanidins, inhibit α-amylase and α-glucosidase—significantly stronger than acarbose in vitro—suggesting utility in postprandial blood glucose control.

plants.name: Chempedak
plants.origin: Southeast Asia: Peninsular Malaysia, Borneo, and parts of Indonesia
plants.economicUse: Edible Fruit: Sweet, fragrant pulp eaten fresh or cooked (especially deep-fried). Seeds are also edible when roasted or boiled. Wood Use: Wood of Artocarpus species is moderately durable and used locally. Processed Products: Chempedak fritters (goreng) are a delicacy in Malaysia and Indonesia.
plants.medicalSignificance: Contains flavonoids and phenolics—antioxidant and antimicrobial properties. Traditionally used to treat fever and skin diseases in some Southeast Asian folk practices. Bark sometimes used in poultices for inflammation

plants.name: Tampoi
plants.origin: Malay Archipelago: Tropical Southeast Asia, especially Malaysia, Indonesia (Borneo, Sumatra), and parts of Thailand
plants.economicUse: Fruit Production: The edible fruit is sweet to slightly acidic, often consumed fresh or used in jams and preserves. Ornamental Value: Grown in tropical gardens for its aesthetic and shade-providing value. Local Markets: Sold in local markets in Southeast Asia, though it's not a major commercial crop.
plants.medicalSignificance: Antioxidant-rich: Due to its vibrant color and bioactive compounds (flavonoids, phenolics). Digestive Aid: Sometimes used to ease stomach issues in traditional practices. Anti-inflammatory: Folk medicine reports topical use for minor swelling or skin issues.

plants.name: Brazilian Mulberry
plants.origin: Western Asia (Persia)
plants.economicUse: Fruits are edible, produces elongated clusters of deep purple to black berries, renowned for their exceptionally sweet, juicy flavor—highly popular for fresh eating, jams, pies, smoothies, and drying. Value‑added Products: Used in syrups, wines, jams, jellies, teas, beverages, desserts, and cosmetic products. Ornamental & Shade Tree with a broad canopy and glossy foliage, often planted in gardens and urban settings.
plants.medicalSignificance:
Rich in Vit-C, minerals, dietary fiber, and water (~88%)—low calorie, moderate sugar.Phytochemicals: High levels of flavonoids, anthocyanins, phenolic compounds. Antioxidant & anti-inflammatory: may protect against oxidative stress, support heart, liver, cognitive health. Hypoglycemic / Anti-diabetic: Compounds especially in leaves inhibit digestive enzymes; fruit and leaf extracts support blood sugar regulation. Antimicrobial: Bark, fruits, leaves show activity against bacteria and fungi; used in traditional formulations and cosmetics for skin health.
Cosmetic uses: Strong tyrosinase inhibition—used in skin‑brightening creams and anti‑aging applications.

plants.name: Alupug
plants.origin: Southeast Asia, particularly the Philippines, but also found in Indonesia, Thailand, and parts of Malaysia
plants.economicUse: Fruits are edible with juicy, aromatic flavour, combining sweetness and mild tartness, somewhat like longan or lychee. Consumption: Typically eaten fresh. Also dried or canned in syrup for preservation. Wood is moderately dense and locally used for making combs or small wooden objects.
plants.medicalSignificance: Vitamin C, potassium, copper, and antioxidants such as epicatechin and rutin. These compounds support immune health, cardiovascular protection, and antioxidant defense. Potential benefits include digestive aid, hydration, and general wellness.

plants.name: Mesta Mangosteen
plants.origin: Southeast Asia, particularly Malaysia
plants.economicUse: Eaten fresh; popular for its exceptional flavor and texture. Horticultural Value: Cultivated by specialty growers; less widespread than standard mangosteen but prized among connoisseurs.
plants.medicalSignificance:
Rich in xanthones, known for antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antimicrobial activity. Has bioactive compounds beneficial for immune support, cardiovascular health, and metabolic regulation, according to general mangosteen research.
Medicinal Use: Traditional use of mangosteen pericarp extracts (not specific to Mesta) includes treatment of diarrhea, skin conditions, and general tonic.

plants.name: Red Ber Apple
plants.origin: South Asia, especially India, Pakistan, and parts of Southeast Asia
plants.economicUse: Eaten ripe that turn glossy bright red, with a sweet-tart flavor and crisp, juicy flesh, sometimes likened to an apple and hence the name. Eaten fresh, or processed into jams, pickles, chutneys, dried snacks.In India, cultivars like "Kashmiri Red Apple Ber" are popular in home gardens and horticulture markets
plants.medicalSignificance: A good source of vitamin C, dietary fiber, and antioxidants. Traditional / Medicinal Uses: Used in folk medicine as an anti-inflammatory and soothing effects. Promoting digestion and supporting immune function. Occasionally used topically for minor skin issues.

plants.name: Kolambu Mango
plants.origin: Sri Lanka (Jaffna region) increasingly popular in Kerala
plants.economicUse: Fruit is eaten fresh, sweet, fragrant, fiberless flesh; high sugar content and excellent taste. It’s renowned for its exceptional flavor and is sought-after in organic fruit markets. Trees are evergreen, with a spreading crown. Primarily consumed fresh; green fruits are used in pickles, chutneys, and local preparations. Exported in small volumes to southern India.
plants.vedicSignificance: Mentioned in Ayurvedic texts under names such as Aamra or Amra. Ripe mango calms Vata and Pitta, while unripe mango—like Kolambu when green—stimulates digestion and balances Vata and Kapha in controlled amounts. Excess can aggravate Pitta or Kapha.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in Vitamins A & C, fiber, minerals, antioxidants. Traditionally used for digestion, blood pressure, calming

plants.name: Jackfruit var. Soft Koozha
plants.vernacularName: Jackfruit var. Soft Koozha / Chunkapura Soft Koozha
plants.origin: Western Ghats and Malayan region
plants.economicUse:
Soft Koozha" refers to jackfruit varieties with soft, juicy, and fibrous bulbs that are very sweet but less crisp than "Varikka" types. Chunkapura/Chunkapara region is known for high-sugar-content Koozha types, with intense aroma and soft melting texture.
Consumed fresh, mashed into jackfruit halwa (chakka varatti), pancakes (ada), and fermented into traditional liquors or vinegar. Seeds are consumed in curries/chutneys.
plants.vedicSignificance: Ayurveda recognizes jackfruit as Panasa (पनस) and describes its: Ripe fruit as Vata-pacifying (sweet, heavy, nourishing). Unripe fruit as Kapha- and Pitta-pacifying (used as a vegetable). Seeds used as digestive and aphrodisiac
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in vitamin C, potassium, dietary fiber, vitamin B6, magnesium, and natural sugars. High-energy fruit; low glycemic load when ripe. Anti-inflammatory, immune-boosting, and antioxidant properties. Traditional use for treating digestive issues, blood pressure, and anemia (due to iron content). Seeds contain thiamine and riboflavin—support nervous system and skin health.

plants.name: Agarwood
plants.origin: Indo-Malayan region, including India, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia
plants.economicUse: Agarwood is the resinous heartwood formed in response to fungal or bacterial infection in Aquilaria trees. Used in perfums, source of the luxurious "oud oil" (attar), used in high-end perfumes, incense, and cosmetics. Used in Buddhist, Islamic, and Hindu rituals. Highly prized in the Middle East and Japan. Woodcraft: Resinous wood chips burned as incense or carved into religious artifacts. Economic Value: One of the most expensive wood products in the world.
plants.vedicSignificance: Mentioned in Ayurveda as Agaru (अगुरु). Found in texts like Charaka Samhita and Sushruta Samhita. Described as deepana (digestive stimulant), hrudya (cardiac tonic), and shirovirechana (nasal cleanser). Often used in herbal oils, dhoop (incense), and medicated ghee preparations.
plants.medicalSignificance: Used in Ayurvedic, Unani, Chinese, and Tibetan medicine. Treats asthma, rheumatism, nervous disorders, digestive problems, and skin ailments. Agarwood oil used topically for relaxation, anti-inflammatory and analgesic effects. Modern Research shows antioxidant, antimicrobial, anti-cancer, and neuroprotective properties. Used in aromatherapy for calming and mental clarity.

plants.name: All-Season Lemon (hybrid)
plants.origin: India and Southeast Asia
plants.economicUse: Eaten fresh: juice used in beverages, pickles, jams, household cleaners, and cosmetics. Particularly valued in home gardens for year-round fruiting and continuous supply of citrus zest and juice.
plants.vedicSignificance: In Ayurveda, lemon is considered "teekshna" (sharp), "laghu" (light), and "ruksha" (dry); it balances kapha and vata, stimulates digestion and absorption, and clears toxins when used in low quantity.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in Vitamin-C, citric acid, and micronutrients; known for antioxidant, antibacterial, and detoxification properties. Used to treat scurvy, improve digestion, relieve respiratory issues, urinary ailments, gum disease, and skin applications. Juice is used as a natural cleaner and disinfectant

plants.name: Guava var. seedless
plants.origin: Central America, the Caribbean, and northern South America
plants.economicUse: Eaten fresh, used in juices, jams, smoothies, desserts, and fruit salads. Same as common guava in shape and color (green, yellow, or pink pulp) making it easier and more pleasant to eat. High pectin content makes regular guava ideal for preserves.
plants.vedicSignificance: Ayurvedic and folk literature, especially its use for digestive health, immunity, oral hygiene, and metabolism.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in vitamin C (often 4–5× that of oranges), dietary fiber, potassium, magnesium, folate, and phytonutrients. Includes quercetin, lycopene (especially in pink/red pulp), carotenoids, flavonoids, and saponins. Antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory, hypoglycemic, anti-hypertensive, digestive aid, cardioprotective, and potentially anticancer. Guava leaf tea and extracts help with diarrhoea, dysentery, oral infections, rheumatism, and skin ailments.

plants.name: Seetaphal
plants.origin: Tropical Americas (Caribbean or Central America)
plants.economicUse: Eaten fresh, sweet, aromatic, and custard-like texture used in milkshakes, ice creams, desserts, and syrups. Seed oil and pulp also used in local skincare and haircare products.
plants.vedicSignificance: Mentioned in Ayurveda: Seetaphala (सीताफल). Dosha effect: Sweet and cooling → balances Vata and Pitta; may aggravate Kapha. Ayurvedic Uses: Fruit: Used to nourish dhatus (tissues), improve strength (balya), and promote vitality. Leaf decoction: Sometimes recommended for fevers and skin diseases. Seeds: Ground and used externally for lice and scalp infections, but never ingested.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in vitamin C, B6, potassium, magnesium, iron, and antioxidants. Fruit pulp: Digestive aid, boosts immunity, relieves constipation, and helps with anemia. Leaves: Used for anti-diabetic, anti-parasitic, and anti-inflammatory properties. Seeds: Traditionally used as insecticidal but toxic if consumed. Root bark: Used in folk medicine for dental problems and skin conditions.

plants.name: Appe Jeerige
plants.botanicalName: Mangifera indica specific cultivar categories Jeerige
plants.origin: Indigenous to the Western Ghats (river valleys of Uttara Kannada, Shimoga, Chikmagalur in Karnataka)
plants.economicUse: Primarily used for making pickles (Appemidi pickles), chutneys, gojju, thambuli, and traditional condiments. The latex exuded acts as a natural preservative, giving pickles long shelf life.
plants.vedicSignificance: Mentioned in In Ayurveda, Mangifera indica is referenced (as Amra/Aamra), and unripe mangoes are especially valued for improving digestion, stimulating appetite, and balancing Kapha and Vata, while being cautiously used for Pitta due to sourness.
plants.medicalSignificance: High in citric acid, antioxidants, and natural latex compounds. Used traditionally in small amounts for digestive stimulation. Medicinal Use: Aids digestion; the sour pulp and latex are believed to support gut health, appetite, and add spice to meals; not a bulk nutritional fruit by itself.

plants.name: Amte
plants.vernacularName: Amte / Ambarella / Hog Plum / Ambade / Ambalo
plants.origin: Melanesia or Polynesia, now widely grown in tropical regions, including South India, Sri Lanka, West Africa, and Caribbean
plants.economicUse: Eaten fresh for its lemony-sour flavor. Popularly used in South Indian cuisine—especially Karnataka—for Amte kai chutney, pickles, and sour tang additions in curries such as Konkani huli (soup) and coastal dishes. Leaves rich in vitamins and fiber contribute to its use in traditional condiments.
plants.vedicSignificance: Mentioned in unriped sour fruit is traditionally employed in Ayurveda to support digestion, balance Kapha, and stimulate Agni (digestive fire).
plants.medicalSignificance: Good source of dietary fiber and vitamin B-complex, along with other micronutrients. Traditional Use: Promotes digestion and adds appetite-enhancing sourness (especially in chutney or curry form). The fruit’s acidity functions as a natural preservative and digestive aid. Used for gastrointestinal support and mild alkalizing effects when consumed in moderation.

plants.name: Longan Berry
plants.origin: Indigenous to Southern China and Northern Vietnam
plants.economicUse: The fruit resembles lychee but is less aromatic, sweeter, and more musk. Fresh consumption (desserts, fruit platters). Dried longan widely used in Chinese and Thai traditional herbal drinks, soups, and sweets. Used in jams, syrups, and as a flavoring in beverages. Major export commodity in Thailand and China.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in vitamin C, iron, potassium, magnesium. Contains polysaccharides and antioxidants. In Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM): considered a tonic to “nourish the blood,” calm the mind, and support sleep. Used to relieve fatigue, palpitations, and anxiety.

plants.name: Mosambi
plants.origin: Mediterranean region or India-Pakistan region
plants.economicUse: Consumed fresh as a fruit or juice (popular street-side juice in India). Used in salads, desserts, and as a flavoring for drinks. Extracted juice is used commercially in the beverage industry. Major economic crop in India with substantial export potential.
plants.vedicSignificance: Mentioned in Ayurveda as Mosambi (or similar sweet citrus) is recognized for its Pitta-pacifying and cooling properties. Recommended for digestive support, balancing excess heat, and rejuvenation.
plants.medicalSignificance: Excellent source of vitamin C, potassium, folate, and dietary fiber. Contains flavonoids and antioxidants. Medicinal Uses: Helps boost immunity due to high vitamin C. Traditionally used to relieve dehydration, indigestion, and nausea. Juice helps soothe sore throat and provides a cooling effect in fevers. Mild diuretic properties.

plants.name: Loquat
plants.origin: South-central China and possibly southern Japan
plants.economicUse: Eaten freah (fruit or pulp) used in jams, jellies, chutneys, pies, syrups, fruit salads, sauces, and smoothies. Fermented use: light fruit wine, seed-based liqueur nespolino (similar to amaretto). Cultivation in India: Grown in states like Punjab, Himachal Pradesh, Maharashtra, Assam, Uttar Pradesh and thriving in subtropical to mild temperate areas.
plants.vedicSignificance: Ayurveda recognized it as Rasa: Sweet and slightly sour (Madhura–Amla). Guna: Light (Laghu), moist (Snigdha). Virya: Cooling (Sheeta).
plants.medicalSignificance: Leaves used as a brewed tea or infusion for respiratory conditions like coughs, bronchitis, and asthma; considered to have anti-inflammatory and expectorant qualities. Fruit: used to halt vomiting and thirst, boost appetite, and soothe digestive discomfort in traditional herbal practices.

plants.name: Orange
plants.origin: Unspecific
plants.economicUse: Grown for small‐fruit yield and compact garden use.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in vitamin C, dietary fiber, and antioxidants; supports heart and brain health.

plants.name: Peach
plants.origin: Northwest China
plants.economicUse: Fresh consumption as table fruit. Processed into canned peaches, jams, jellies, juices, desserts. Used in baking (pies, cobblers), beverages, and flavoring. Major commercial fruit crop in countries like China, USA, Italy, Spain, and India.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich source of vitamins A and C, dietary fiber, potassium. Has antioxidants like chlorogenic acid and flavonoids. Medicinal Uses: Supports skin health and immune system. Aids digestion due to fiber content. Traditional use includes mild laxative and diuretic effects. Contains compounds with anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties.

plants.name: Cardamom
plants.origin: Tropical forests of southern India, Sri Lanka, and possibly parts of Southeast Asia
plants.economicUse: Widely used as a spice and flavoring agent in cooking, baking, and beverages (tea, coffee). Used in traditional medicine and perfumery. Important export commodity for India, Guatemala, Sri Lanka, and other tropical countries.
plants.vedicSignificance: Cardamom is mentioned in classical Ayurvedic texts as a valuable spice and medicinal herb. It is considered Ushna (warming) in potency and helps balance Kapha and Vata doshas. Used to treat digestive issues, respiratory problems, and as a rejuvenating herb.
plants.medicalSignificance: Traditionally used to aid digestion, relieve stomach discomfort, and reduce nausea. Has antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and antioxidant properties. Used in Ayurveda to improve respiratory health, relieve cold symptoms, and detoxify the body. Often used as a breath freshener.

plants.name: Papaya
plants.origin: Southern Mexico and Central America
plants.economicUse: Eaten fresh or in fruit salads, smoothies, desserts. Used in cooking (raw green papaya in salads and stews). Papain enzyme extracted for meat tenderizers, cosmetics, and pharmaceuticals. Seeds sometimes used as a spice substitute with peppery flavor.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in vitamin C, vitamin A (beta-carotene), folate, potassium, fiber, and antioxidants. Medicinal Uses: Aids digestion due to papain enzyme that breaks down proteins. Supports immune function, skin health, and reduces inflammation. Used traditionally to treat digestive disorders, reduce constipation, and promote wound healing. Seeds have antimicrobial and antiparasitic properties.

plants.name: Clove
plants.origin: Native to the Maluku Islands (Spice Islands) in Indonesia
plants.economicUse: Widely used as a spice in Indian, Middle Eastern, and global cuisines. Used whole or ground in curries, rice dishes, pickles, and desserts. Clove oil is used in perfumery, cosmetics, dental preparations, and pharmaceuticals. It is a valuable export spice crop in countries like Indonesia, India, Sri Lanka, and Madagascar.
plants.vedicSignificance: Found in classic Ayurvedic texts like Charaka Samhita and Sushruta Samhita. It si considered: Ushna (hot in potency), Deepana (appetizer), Pachana (digestive), Kaphahara & Vatahara (reduces Kapha and Vata doshas). It is used in Ayurvedic remedies for: Toothache, bad breath, indigestion and bloating, cough, cold, and respiratory congestion.
plants.medicalSignificance:
Dental Relief: Clove oil is a natural analgesic and antiseptic; used for toothaches, gum pain. 
Digestive Aid: Stimulates enzyme secretion, relieves bloating and gas. 
Antimicrobial: Eugenol (main active compound) is antifungal, antibacterial, and antiviral. 
Anti-inflammatory: Helps reduce inflammation in arthritis, infections. 
Respiratory Health: Eases cough, bronchitis, and asthma symptoms.

plants.name: Babbugosha
plants.origin: Europe and Western Asia; cultivated widely in India
plants.economicUse: Consumed as a fresh fruit for its sweet, mildly grainy texture. Used in fruit salads, desserts, jams, juices, and purees. Horticultural Value: Grown commercially for local markets due to good shelf life and transportability. Agro-Industrial: Juice and pulp used in beverages and baby foods. Dried slices sometimes used in trail mixes.
plants.vedicSignificance: Not explicitly mentioned in Ayurveda but konwn as Phala Varga (fruit group) and are valued for: Tridosha balancing (especially cooling for Pitta) Mridu, Snigdha (gentle, soft) properties. Recognized in Unani and Tibbi medicine for: Cooling, moistening effect on the body: Beneficial in digestive and urinary issues.
plants.medicalSignificance:
Digestive Health: High in dietary fiber; helps regulate bowel movement and relieve constipation.
Hydration & Cooling: Rich in water and cooling nature—good for summer & Pitta disorders.
Heart Health: Contains potassium, antioxidants, and fiber that support cardiovascular health.
Weight Management: Low in calories, high in fiber—helps with satiety and digestion.
Diabetes-Friendly: Low glycemic index; helps regulate blood sugar (in moderation).
Anti-inflammatory	Contains flavonoids with inflammation-reducing effects.

plants.name: Nashpati
plants.vernacularName: Nashpati / Asian Pear / Japanese Pear / Chinese Pear / Sand Pear
plants.origin: Southern China and northern Indochina, later introduced extensively to Japan, Korea, Nepal, and northern Indian hill regions
plants.economicUse: Highly valued for its large, crisp, grainy, juicy fruit—often served fresh or presented as premium gifts in East Asia and the Himalayan foothills. Used as a natural sweetener and meat tenderizer (notably in Korean bulgogi marinade) due to its enzyme content; lightly cooked fruits also feature in Nepalese and Himachali dishes.
plants.vedicSignificance: Mentioned in Ayurveda by names like Nashpathi, occasionally as Amrithaphala. Traditionally in Ayurvedic literature mentions its cooling, digestive, anti-dysenteric, anti-inflammatory uses; leaves and bark noted for wound healing – while modern Ayurvedic writers describe naspati in a context analogous to its current use.
plants.medicalSignificance: Vitamin C/E/K & B vitamins; fiber-rich; Ayurvedic uses — digestive aid, cooling, anti‑inflammatory, wound healing, metabolic support.

plants.name: Almond
plants.origin: Central and Southwest Asia (Iran, Afghanistan)
plants.economicUse: Eaten raw, soaked, roasted, or in sweets. Used in almond milk, flour, oil, butter, and desserts (e.g. badam halwa, marzipan). Almond oil in cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, and massage therapy. Almond shell used in activated carbon, biomass, and eco-products. A major global nut crop (California, Spain, Iran, Italy, India—especially J&K and Himachal)
plants.vedicSignificance: Mentioned in Ayurveda. Snigdha (unctuous), Guru (heavy), Madhura (sweet). Balances Vata and Pitta, can increase Kapha if taken in excess. Ayurvedic Uses: Medhya rasayana – brain tonic. Used for reproductive strength, vitality, and skin enhancement. Strengthens ojas (vital essence), recommended in convalescence.
plants.medicalSignificance:
Brain Function: Rich in riboflavin and L-carnitine; supports memory and cognition.
Heart Health: High in monounsaturated fats; helps reduce LDL (bad cholesterol).
Skin & Hair: Almond oil nourishes skin, reduces dryness, and promotes healthy hair.
Diabetes Support: Lowers post-meal blood sugar spikes due to low glycemic load
Bone Health: Excellent source of magnesium, phosphorus, and calcium.
Weight Management: Provides satiety and healthy fats for balanced energy.

plants.name: Lakshmi Tharu
plants.origin: Tropical regions of Central America, particularly Florida
plants.economicUse: Wasteland reclamation and carbon sequestration. Used as a soil amendment. Leaves, bark, seed, fruit pulp, leaf litter, branches, and root are utilized in producing food supplements, fuel, manure, timber, medicinal extracts, and organic mulch.
plants.medicalSignificance:
Traditional uses include treatment of dysentery, diarrhea, malaria, colitis, fever, edema, wounds, dyspepsia, and as a tonic, febrifuge, emmenagogue, vermifuge, astringent, and wound healer. 
Pharmacological activities attributed to the plant include antiviral, antibacterial, antidysenteric, antileukemic, antimalarial, antimicrobial, cytotoxic (anti-cancer), and anti‑tumor effects.

plants.name: Burmese grape
plants.origin: Southeast Asia — India (Assam, Andaman & Nicobar Islands), Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Vietnam, Malaysia, South China
plants.economicUse:
Eaten Fruits are eaten fresh, stewed, or fermented into wine; valued for their sour‑sweet translucent pulp and seeds which can also be consumed.
Industrial/utilitarian: Fruit rind contains pectin used for jams and jellies; seeds yield omega‑9 rich oil and annatto dye; pulp can be processed into functional foods.
plants.medicalSignificance: Used in folk medicine for treating jaundice, constipation, indigestion, skin infections, abscesses, anemia, rheumatoid arthritis, pain, and as an antivenom. Bioactive effects: Research indicates analgesic, anti-inflammatory, thrombolytic, hypolipidemic, antimicrobial, cytotoxic (possible anticancer), antidiarrheal, neuropharmacological activities;

plants.name: Cuppassu
plants.origin: Amazon Basin espacially Northern Brazil, Colombia, Peru, Bolivia
plants.economicUse:
Culinary: The white pulp is used in cuisines. Used in juices, smoothies, ice creams, jams, mousses, and a chocolate-like product called “cupulate”. 
Agroforestry Crop: Commonly grown in shaded mixed-crop systems across the Amazon due to its adaptability to low-nutrient soils.
plants.medicalSignificance:
High in vitamins A, B1, B2, B3, C, and E, essential fatty acids (omega‑3, omega‑6, omega‑9), fiber, proteins, calcium, selenium, iron, potassium, and amino acids. Contains flavonoids, polyphenols (theograndins, catechins, quercetin, kaempferol, epicatechin), tannins, and mild alkaloids (theacrine, theobromine, theophylline).
Skin & Hair Care: Cupuaçu butter deeply hydrates skin (retaining up to 450% its weight in water), restores elasticity, and soothes dry or aging skin; also improves hair hydration and minimizes damage. May help regulate blood sugar, cholesterol, and blood pressure owing to flavonoids like quercetin and epicatechin. Contains theacrine and caffeine-like compounds (lower than cacao) for sustained mental alertness without jitters. It is a potential Anti-Cancer: Early studies suggest anticancer activity in cell models.

plants.name: Sweet Kokam
plants.vernacularName: Sweet Kokam / Malabar Tamarind / Bindin / Aamsul
plants.origin: Western Ghats of India, especially Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka
plants.economicUse: Fruit rind is used as a natural souring agent in Indian cuisine (similar to tamarind). Sweet Kokam syrup is made from the ripe fruit juice and sugar. Used in summer coolers and sherbets. Kokam butter (extracted from seeds) is used in cosmetics, confectionery, and pharmaceuticals. Agroforestry: Valued as a hardy fruit tree in marginal lands.
plants.vedicSignificance:
Mentioned in Ayurvedic texts under names like:
Vrikshamla, Amlabija, or Sour fruit. Known for:
Deepana (digestive stimulant). Pachana (digestive). Rochana (appetite stimulant)
plants.medicalSignificance:
Digestive aid: Stimulates appetite, relieves indigestion and flatulence. Anti-obesity: Hydroxycitric acid (HCA) in the rind is believed to aid in weight loss.
Anti-inflammatory: Used traditionally for arthritis and inflammatory conditions.
Cardioprotective: Antioxidants help reduce oxidative stress on the heart.
Antioxidant: Rich in anthocyanins, beneficial for overall health.
Skin & Wound healing	Kokam butter soothes dry skin, burns, and chapped lips.
Cooling agent: Traditional summer remedy to prevent heat strokes and dehydration.

plants.name: Chop Chop
plants.origin: Tropical regions of the Americas and the Caribbean—primarily native to Mexico, Central America, northern South America (e.g. Colombia, Brazil, Peru)
plants.economicUse:
Eaten raw in ripe form for its sweet-sour, creamy pulp (texture reminiscent of strawberry/pineapple/banana). 
Used to make beverages, smoothies, ice creams, and juices due to its aromatic pulp. 
Industrial Use: The tree is also cultivated commercially for fruit markets and potential medicinal extracts (e.g., leaf extracts and supplements).
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in nutrients: vitamins C, B1 (thiamin), B2 (riboflavin), fiber, iron, calcium, potassium, and phosphorus. Contains unique phytochemicals: Annonaceous acetogenins, which have shown cytotoxic activity against various cancer cells in lab studies.

plants.name: Golden mooty
plants.origin: Western Ghats of India
plants.economicUse: The evergreen tree with a low, dense crown is also cultivated for ornamental purposes and shade.
plants.medicalSignificance: There is limited published pharmacological or clinical research on B. courtallensis, unlike its relative Baccaurea ramiflora (Burmese grape).

plants.name: Persimmon
plants.origin: China, Japan, Taiwan (East Asia)
plants.economicUse: Eaten fresh or dried. Used in desserts, jams, puddings, and baked goods. Sometimes used in alcoholic beverages like persimmon wine or vinegar. Wood from Diospyros species is used in fine woodworking.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in antioxidants: Especially vitamin C, beta-carotene, lutein, and lycopene. Supports heart health: Due to potassium and flavonoids. High in fiber: Helps in digestion and bowel regulation. Anti-inflammatory: Contains tannins and polyphenols. Eye health: High vitamin A content supports vision. Anti-cancer potential: Some studies suggest antioxidant compounds may reduce cancer risk.

plants.name: Blackberry
plants.origin: Europe and North America (widespread across temperate regions)
plants.economicUse: Consumed fresh or processed into jams, jellies, syrups, and desserts. Used in wines, juices, and flavored liquors. Dried blackberries used in teas or health snacks. Leaves used traditionally for herbal teas and medicinal purposes.
plants.medicalSignificance: High in antioxidants: Anthocyanins and vitamin C protect cells from damage. Supports brain function: Flavonoids may improve memory and cognition. Rich in fiber: Aids digestion and supports gut health. Anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial: Especially from blackberry leaf extracts. May support heart health: Due to polyphenols and fiber content. Good for oral health: Leaves used in traditional remedies for mouth ulcers and sore throats.

plants.name: Cinnamon
plants.origin: Sri Lanka and Southern India
plants.economicUse: Widely used as a spice in culinary dishes, baking, and beverages. Used in essential oils, perfumery, and cosmetics. Important in traditional medicine and Ayurvedic formulations. Preservative and flavoring agent in food industries.
plants.vedicSignificance: Widely used as a spice in culinary dishes, baking, and beverages. Used in essential oils, perfumery, and cosmetics. Important in traditional medicine and Ayurvedic formulations. Preservative and flavoring agent in food industries.
plants.medicalSignificance: Antioxidant-rich: Protects against cell damage. Antimicrobial: Effective against bacteria and fungi. Blood sugar control: May reduce insulin resistance. Digestive aid: Stimulates appetite and reduces bloating. Anti-inflammatory: Helps with joint pain and swelling. Heart health: May lower cholesterol and triglycerides.

plants.name: Bush Pepper
plants.origin: Western Ghats of India
plants.economicUse:
Spice production: Dried berries used as black pepper.
Grown on a small scale for home use or nursery trade.
A good source of income in urban and peri-urban home gardening models. Used in pickles, seasoning, and traditional medicine.
plants.vedicSignificance: Widely mentioned in Ayurveda, as “Maricha” (मरिच). Found in classical texts like Charaka Samhita, Sushruta Samhita. Part of Trikatu (a classical Ayurvedic formulation of three pungent herbs: black pepper, long pepper, and ginger). Used for: Stimulating digestion, Treating respiratory disorders, Enhancing bioavailability of other herbs.
plants.medicalSignificance: Digestive stimulant – boosts appetite, relieves bloating and flatulence. Bioavailability enhancer – piperine increases absorption of nutrients and drugs. Antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. Respiratory support – helps with cough, asthma, and bronchitis. Antimicrobial – combats infections and improves immunity.

plants.name: Tej Patta
plants.origin: Indian subcontinent (Himalayan region – India, Nepal, Bhutan)
plants.economicUse: Widely used as a culinary spice (especially in Indian cuisine) for its aromatic flavor. Leaves used in curries, biryanis, soups, and spice mixes. Also used in essential oils, perfumery, and traditional medicine.
plants.vedicSignificance: Extensively used in Ayurveda as Tamala Patra or Patra. Mentioned in Charaka Samhita, Sushruta Samhita, and other classical texts. Known to: Stimulate digestion, Alleviate respiratory disorders. Act as a carminative and mild diuretic
plants.medicalSignificance: Digestive aid – helps with bloating, gas, and poor appetite. Antimicrobial and antifungal – due to essential oils like eugenol and cinnamaldehyde. Respiratory health – helps relieve cough and cold. Antioxidant – protects against free radical damage. Blood sugar support – traditionally used for mild diabetic control.

plants.name: Peach
plants.origin: Northwest China (specifically the Yangtze River valley)
plants.economicUse: Consumed fresh, canned, dried, or juiced. Used in desserts, jams, jellies, and baked goods. Important commercial fruit crop worldwide. Also used in cosmetics and flavoring.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in vitamins: Especially vitamin C and A (beta-carotene). Antioxidant properties: Helps combat oxidative stress. Good source of dietary fiber: Aids digestion. Supports heart health: Contains potassium and flavonoids. Hydrating fruit: High water content helps in hydration.

plants.name: Dragonfruit
plants.origin: Native to Central America (Mexico, Guatemala, Costa Rica)
plants.economicUse: Consumed fresh or in smoothies, juices, salads, and desserts. Used in jams, ice creams, and health drinks. Popular as an exotic fruit worldwide, especially in tropical/subtropical countries. Grown commercially in Southeast Asia (Vietnam, Thailand), Israel, Australia, and the USA.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in antioxidants: Vitamin C, betalains, and carotenoids. High fiber content: Aids digestion and promotes gut health. Supports immune system: Vitamin C boosts immunity. Low calorie: Suitable for weight management. Good source of magnesium and iron.

plants.name: Pomegranate
plants.origin: Native to Iran to northern India (Middle East region)
plants.economicUse: Consumed fresh or as juice, syrup (grenadine), and in culinary dishes. Used in jams, jellies, sauces, and alcoholic beverages. Seeds (arils) and peel used in traditional medicine and cosmetics. Cultivated worldwide in tropical and subtropical climates.
plants.vedicSignificance: Extensively mentioned in Ayurveda as Dadimba. Referenced in Charaka Samhita, Sushruta Samhita, and other classical texts. Used for balancing all three doshas, especially Kapha and Pitta. Used in treatments for: Digestive disorders, Skin diseases, Respiratory ailments, Parasitic infections.
plants.medicalSignificance: Antioxidant-rich: High in polyphenols and vitamin C. Anti-inflammatory: Useful in arthritis and other inflammatory conditions. Heart health: Helps reduce blood pressure and cholesterol. Digestive health: Aids in digestion and gut microbiota balance. Antimicrobial: Effective against bacteria, fungi, and parasites. Anti-cancer potential: Studied for effects on certain cancer cells.

plants.name: Bakery Cherry
plants.origin: Europe, North Africa, and Western Asia
plants.economicUse: Fruits used fresh, dried, or as a spice in cooking (especially in Middle Eastern and Persian cuisines). Used in jams, jellies, sauces, and herbal teas. Wood used for dye and traditional medicine. Cultivated for ornamental purposes in gardens.
plants.medicalSignificance: Antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory due to berberine alkaloid. Digestive aid – improves liver and gallbladder function. Blood sugar regulation – helps in diabetes management. Antioxidant – protects cells from oxidative stress. Skin health – used for wounds and infections.

plants.name: Rudrakshi
plants.origin: Himalayan region (India, Nepal, Bhutan) and parts of Southeast Asia
plants.economicUse: Seeds (called beads) used extensively in spiritual and religious practices, especially in Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism. Used for making prayer malas (rosaries) and jewelry. Also valued in traditional medicine. Growing demand for Rudrakshi beads in spiritual and wellness markets globally.
plants.vedicSignificance: Mentioned in Puranas and ancient Hindu scriptures. Considered sacred, believed to have divine origin (associated with Lord Shiva). Used in meditation and prayer for mental peace, spiritual growth, and protection. Ayurveda attributes healing properties to Rudrakshi beads, especially for nervous system and stress relief.
plants.medicalSignificance: Calming effect: Helps reduce stress, anxiety, and nervous tension. Spiritual aid: Enhances concentration, meditation, and mental clarity. Balancing energies: Believed to balance chakras and energy flows. Anti-inflammatory: Traditionally used in some Ayurvedic remedies. Cardiovascular benefits: Some believe it helps regulate blood pressure and heart rate.

plants.name: Madhu Malthil
plants.origin: East Asia (Japan, China, Korea)
plants.economicUse: Grown as an ornamental climbing plant for its fragrant flowers. Used in traditional medicine in East Asia, particularly Chinese herbal medicine. Sometimes cultivated for honey production because of its nectar-rich flowers.
plants.medicalSignificance: Flowers and leaves are used in traditional medicine for: Reducing fever, Treating inflammation, Respiratory infections (like cough, sore throat), Skin infections and wounds (topical use), Has antibacterial, anti-inflammatory, and antioxidant properties.

plants.name: Drumstick
plants.origin: Northwestern India and the Himalayan foothills
plants.economicUse: Edible parts are Pods (drumsticks), leaves, flowers, and seeds are consumed as vegetables. Leaves and seeds used in nutraceuticals, health supplements, and protein powders. Oil is extracted from seeds used in cooking, cosmetics, and lubrication. Grown as a fast-growing, drought-resistant tree for fencing, erosion control, and green manure.
plants.vedicSignificance: Mentioned in Ayurveda and known as Shigru. Extensively mentioned in classical Ayurvedic texts such as Charaka Samhita and Bhavaprakasha. Used for: Balancing Vata and Kapha doshas, enhancing digestion, managing joint pain and inflammation, detoxification.
plants.medicalSignificance: Anti-inflammatory: Used in arthritis and swelling. Rich in nutrients: High in vitamins A, C, calcium, iron, and protein. Antioxidant and antimicrobial: Supports immune function. Blood sugar regulation: Helps manage diabetes. Liver support and detox: Improves liver function and eliminates toxins. Cardiovascular health: Helps reduce cholesterol and supports heart function.

plants.name: Grapes
plants.origin: Near East and Central Asia (Mediterranean region, including present-day Iran, Turkey, Armenia)
plants.economicUse: Grown for fresh consumption (table grapes), raisins, juice, and especially wine production. Seed oil used in cosmetics and culinary applications. Important crop in viticulture and winemaking industries globally. Used in jams, jellies, vinegar, and health supplements.
plants.vedicSignificance: Known as Draksha in Ayurveda. Mentioned in ancient texts for: Rejuvenation, Cooling and energizing properties, Balancing Pitta dosha, Used in Draksharishta, an Ayurvedic herbal wine for digestive and respiratory ailments.
plants.medicalSignificance: Antioxidant-rich: Contains resveratrol, flavonoids, and polyphenols beneficial for heart and cellular health. Supports heart health: Lowers blood pressure and improves circulation. Digestive aid: Mild laxative; aids digestion. Respiratory health: Used in remedies for cough, asthma, and bronchitis. Anti-aging & skin care: Promotes youthful skin and detoxification. Hydrating and energizing: Natural source of glucose and water.

plants.name: Aloe vera
plants.origin: Arabian Peninsula, but widely cultivated worldwide in tropical and subtropical regions
plants.economicUse: Widely used in cosmetics, skin care, and personal care products (gels, lotions, creams). Used in traditional medicine for skin and digestive health. Cultivated commercially for extracting aloe gel and juice. Also used in beverages, dietary supplements, and food industry.
plants.vedicSignificance: Mentioned as Kumari in Ayurvedic texts like Charaka Samhita and Sushruta Samhita. Used for: Healing skin disorders, Digestive health, Detoxification, Wound healing.
plants.medicalSignificance: Skin healing: Treats burns, wounds, psoriasis, and eczema. Anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial: Reduces inflammation and fights infections. Digestive aid: Helps with constipation and gut health. Immune booster: Contains antioxidants and vitamins. Hydrating and soothing: Used in cosmetics for moisturizing.

plants.name: Starfruit
plants.origin: Southeast Asia (particularly Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines)
plants.economicUse: Eaten fresh or used in salads, juices, pickles, jams, chutneys. Used in beverages and garnishing due to its attractive star shape when sliced. Grown commercially in tropical and subtropical regions. Occasionally used in traditional cleaning or polishing due to its oxalic acid content.
plants.vedicSignificance: Known in Ayurveda and traditional systems by names like Kamrakh (Hindi) or Karmal (Sanskrit-based). Not a major classical Ayurvedic herb, but used in folk and Unani systems. Believed to help balance Pitta and Kapha.
plants.medicalSignificance: Digestive aid: Stimulates digestion and relieves constipation (in moderation). Anti-inflammatory: Helps in reducing swelling and pain. Rich in vitamin C: Boosts immunity and acts as an antioxidant. Diuretic effect: Helps in flushing out toxins. Used in diabetes management in folk medicine (with caution). Supports skin health and acts as a mild liver tonic.

plants.name: Kiwi Fruit
plants.origin: China (Yangtze River Valley region)
plants.economicUse: Consumed fresh or used in salads, juices, desserts, jams, jellies, smoothies. Widely cultivated for export markets—notably in New Zealand, Italy, Chile, and India. Used in the cosmetic and nutraceutical industries due to its vitamin C and antioxidant content. High market value due to nutritional richness and appeal as an exotic fruit.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in Vitamin C: Boosts immunity and skin health. High in dietary fiber: Aids digestion and prevents constipation. Antioxidant properties: Fights oxidative stress and aging. Good for heart health: Regulates blood pressure and lowers cholesterol. Low glycemic index: Suitable for diabetic diets in moderation. Aids in iron absorption: Especially beneficial in iron-deficiency anemia.

plants.name: Blueberry
plants.origin: North America (particularly USA and Canada). Wild blueberries are also found in parts of Europe and Asia
plants.economicUse: Consumed fresh, in juices, jams, baking, and desserts. Used in food supplements and cosmetics. High commercial value due to antioxidant-rich nature. Cultivated as a cash crop in temperate zones globally
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in antioxidants (especially anthocyanins). Supports brain health, memory, and may help delay age-related decline. Aids in reducing inflammation. Supports heart health and lowers bad cholesterol. Helps regulate blood sugar levels. Promotes eye health. May help improve gut health.

plants.name: Redcherry
plants.origin: Europe and Western Asia
plants.economicUse: Eaten fresh, in juices, preserves, desserts, baked goods, and ice creams. Used in wine, liqueurs, and confectionery. Wood of cherry trees used in furniture making. High-value export fruit.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in antioxidants (like anthocyanins and quercetin).Anti-inflammatory properties; may help with arthritis and gout. Supports heart health. Helps improve sleep quality due to natural melatonin. May aid in exercise recovery. Good for skin health and anti-aging

plants.name: Black Jamun
plants.vernacularName: Black Jamun / Java Plum / Indian Blackberry / Jambolan / Jamun / Jambu
plants.origin: Indian subcontinent, Southeast Asia
plants.economicUse: Consumed fresh or in juices, vinegar, squash, jelly, and wine. Seeds used in Ayurvedic medicines and nutraceuticals. Wood used for making furniture, agricultural implements, and railway sleepers. A source of natural dye.
plants.vedicSignificance: Known as “Jambu” or “Jambava” in Ayurvedic texts. Described in Charaka Samhita and Sushruta Samhita. Balances Kapha and Pitta doshas. Used in formulations like Jambavasava, Jambu Churna.
plants.medicalSignificance: Excellent for diabetes management – regulates blood sugar (seed powder especially effective). Acts as a digestive aid – reduces acidity, flatulence. Possesses astringent, anti-inflammatory, and antioxidant properties. Beneficial in urinary disorders. Improves skin health and helps treat acne. Rich in vitamin C, iron, and flavonoids.

plants.name: Curry Leaves
plants.vernacularName: Curry Leaves / Karipatta / Kadhi Patta /Meetha Neem
plants.origin: India and Sri Lanka. Native to tropical and subtropical regions of South Asia
plants.economicUse: Widely used as a culinary herb in Indian, Sri Lankan, and Southeast Asian cuisine. Added for flavor and aroma in curries, dals, and rice dishes. Leaves, bark, and roots used in Ayurvedic and Siddha medicines. Cultivated for essential oil (used in cosmetics and perfumes). Can be grown in home gardens and plantations.
plants.vedicSignificance: Known as “Krishna Nimba” or “Kadi Patra” in Ayurveda. Mentioned in Ayurvedic pharmacopoeia for its medicinal properties. Balances Vata and Kapha doshas
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in iron, calcium, vitamin A, vitamin C, and carbazole alkaloids. Improves digestion and helps relieve nausea, constipation, and diarrhea. Supports hair growth and prevents premature greying. Controls blood sugar levels – useful for diabetics. Contains antioxidant, antibacterial, and anti-inflammatory properties. May protect liver function and reduce cholesterol.

plants.name: Velvet Apple
plants.vernacularName: Velvet Apple / Mabolo / Butter Fruit / Peach Bloom / Kamagong
plants.origin: Native to the Philippines. Also found in Indonesia, Malaysia, and Sri Lanka
plants.economicUse: Grown for its edible fruit, which has a soft, creamy pulp with a cheesy or custard-like flavor. The timber (called Kamagong) is extremely dense, dark, and valuable, used in furniture, swords, and flooring. Cultivated in tropical gardens as an ornamental and fruit tree.
plants.medicalSignificance: Antioxidant-rich – contains vitamin A, C, B-complex, and fiber. Supports digestive health – natural laxative. May help lower cholesterol and improve heart health. Used in folk medicine to treat diarrhea, dysentery, and hypertension. Leaf extracts have shown antibacterial and anti-inflammatory properties in studies. Fruit is good for skin, eyes, and immune system.

plants.name: Governor’s plum
plants.vernacularName: Governor’s plum / Indian Plum / Otumpa / Rukun / Koklikham
plants.origin: Tropical Africa and South and Southeast Asia
plants.economicUse: Fruits eaten raw or made into jams, jellies, juices, and wine. Grown as hedge plant—due to its thorny branches. Used in reforestation, live fencing, and erosion control. Timber is used for agricultural tools and firewood.
plants.vedicSignificance: Known in Ayurveda and Siddha systems as “Vikankataka” or “Koklikham”. Used traditionally for treating wounds, digestive disorders, and skin infections. Balances Pitta and Kapha doshas. Also mentioned in folk medicine for antipyretic and analgesic effects.
plants.medicalSignificance: Antibacterial, antifungal, and antioxidant properties. Used to treat diarrhea, fever, stomach aches, and ulcers. Bark and leaves used in decoctions for wound healing and skin diseases. Helps manage blood sugar and supports liver health. Leaf extracts may help reduce inflammation and pain. Fruit is mildly astringent and supports digestive health.

plants.name: Red Pomelo
plants.origin: Southeast Asia (Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Philippines)
plants.economicUse: Consumed fresh as fruit, in salads, juices, and desserts. Used in traditional festivals and as an ornamental fruit. The peel used for candied fruit, essential oils, and traditional medicine. Cultivated commercially in Asia, Florida, and other citrus-growing regions.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in vitamin C, fiber, antioxidants, and flavonoids. Supports immune function and helps prevent common colds. Promotes heart health by lowering cholesterol and blood pressure. Aids digestion and promotes weight management. Contains anti-inflammatory and anticancer potential compounds. May improve skin health and reduce signs of aging.

plants.name: Pears
plants.origin: European pear native to Europe and Western Asia. Asian pear native to East Asia (China, Japan, Korea)
plants.economicUse: Consumed fresh, in canned products, juices, desserts, salads, and baked goods. Used in fermentation for perry (pear cider) production. Cultivated commercially worldwide with major producers including China, USA, Italy, and Argentina.
plants.vedicSignificance: Pears are mentioned in Ayurveda primarily as a cooling fruit. Used to balance Pitta dosha and sometimes recommended for digestive health. Known for being easy to digest and beneficial for respiratory health.
plants.medicalSignificance: High in dietary fiber, which aids digestion and promotes bowel regularity. Rich in vitamin C, potassium, and antioxidants. May help reduce inflammation and support heart health. Hydrating fruit, helps maintain skin health and kidney function. Contains phytonutrients that support immune function and may reduce risk of chronic diseases.

plants.name: Kudampali
plants.vernacularName: Kudampali / Nutgrass / Purple Nutgrass / Khadira grass
plants.origin: Africa, Asia, and parts of Europe
plants.economicUse: Considered a weed in agriculture but used in traditional medicine. Rhizomes used as aromatic ingredient in perfumes and incense. Extracts used in cosmetics and natural remedies.
plants.vedicSignificance: Known as “Musta” in Ayurveda. Highly valued in Ayurvedic medicine for its digestive, anti-inflammatory, and diuretic properties. Balances Vata and Kapha doshas. Used in formulations for fevers, digestive disorders, menstrual issues, and pain relief.
plants.medicalSignificance: Promotes digestion, relieves indigestion, and reduces gas and bloating. Has anti-inflammatory, analgesic, antimicrobial, and antioxidant effects. Used for menstrual cramps, fever, skin conditions, and wound healing. May help regulate blood sugar and support weight management. Traditionally used to treat urinary tract infections and respiratory ailments.

plants.name: Walnut
plants.origin: Persian region (Iran, surrounding areas)
plants.economicUse: Valued for its edible nuts, consumed raw, roasted, or as ingredient in cooking and baking. Wood used in fine furniture, gunstocks, and carvings. Walnut oil extracted for culinary and cosmetic uses.
plants.vedicSignificance: Known as “Akhrot” in Ayurveda.Used traditionally as a brain tonic and to supports nervous system health. Balances Vata and Kapha doshas. Mentioned in Ayurvedic texts for strengthening the body and improving memory.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in omega-3 fatty acids, antioxidants, vitamins (E, B6), and minerals (magnesium, copper).Supports heart health by lowering bad cholesterol (LDL).Improves brain function and cognitive health. Anti-inflammatory and may help reduce risk of chronic diseases. Supports weight management and metabolic health. Contains polyphenols that protect against oxidative stress.

plants.name: Lime Berry
plants.origin: India and Pakistan
plants.economicUse: Grown for its edible berries, which are sweet-sour and refreshing. Consumed fresh, in juices, jellies, and traditional drinks. Popular in summer for its cooling effect. Sometimes used as fodder and in traditional medicine.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in vitamin C, antioxidants, and fiber. Helps reduce heat stress and body temperature. Aids digestion and may help with constipation. Exhibits anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial properties. Used to treat respiratory issues, skin diseases, and fever.

plants.name: Candle Fruit
plants.vernacularName: Candle Fruit / Ivy Gourd / Tindora / Kundru / Kovakkai
plants.origin: Tropical Asia and Africa
plants.economicUse: Cultivated as a vegetable for its immature green fruits. Used in stir-fries, curries, pickles, and salads. Popular in Indian, Thai, Filipino, and African cuisines. Sometimes used in traditional medicine.
plants.vedicSignificance: Known in Ayurveda as Tindora or Kundru. Used for its cooling and digestive properties. Balances Pitta and Kapha doshas. Often included in treatments for diabetes, fever, and skin diseases.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in vitamins A and C, iron, and fiber. Helps regulate blood sugar levels—used as a natural remedy for diabetes. Supports digestion and weight management. Exhibits antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antimicrobial properties. Traditionally used to treat urinary tract infections, skin disorders, and fever.

plants.name: Sambarballi
plants.origin: India and Southeast Asia
plants.economicUse: Consumed fresh, dried, or as juice, powder, and supplements. Used in Ayurvedic medicine and hair care products. Key ingredient in churna (herbal powders) and rasayanas.
plants.vedicSignificance: Highly valued in Ayurveda as a rejuvenator (Rasayana). Balances all three doshas (Vata, Pitta, Kapha). Described extensively for its immune-boosting, digestive, and detoxifying properties.
plants.medicalSignificance: Extremely rich in vitamin C and antioxidants. Supports immune system, digestion, and liver health. Anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, and promotes skin and hair health. Used to treat diabetes, respiratory disorders, and cardiovascular health. Acts as a natural detoxifier and supports anti-aging.

plants.name: Bombay Nelli
plants.vernacularName: Bombay Nelli / Star Gooseberry / Otaheite Gooseberry / Malay Gooseberry
plants.origin: Madagascar or India–Malaysia region
plants.economicUse: Fruits are used in pickles, chutneys, jams, and preserves. Occasionally eaten raw (very sour). Wood used in tool handles and carving.
plants.vedicSignificance: Known in Ayurveda as a cooling and detoxifying fruit. Used traditionally for digestive health, bile regulation, and skin conditions. Helps balance Pitta and Kapha doshas.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in vitamin C, antioxidants, and flavonoids. Acts as a liver tonic and promotes digestion. Used for treating fever, constipation, cough, and skin infections. Has anti-inflammatory, antibacterial, and antioxidant properties. Traditionally used to purify blood and support immunity.

plants.name: Jagma Cherry
plants.vernacularName: Jagma Cherry / Jamaican Cherry / Panama Cherry / Strawberry Tree
plants.origin: Central and South America, but now naturalized throughout the tropics
