plants.economicUse: Made into jams, jellies, and used in desserts or infused beverages. Flowers are used as tea-like infusions and have mild medicinal use; tree thrives easily in low-maintenance settings.
plants.vedicSignificance: Valued as antispasmodic and antiseptic; used to relieve headaches and mild cold symptoms. IIn folk/traditional medicine, leaves and roots have been used for minor ailments, but formal documented uses are limited.
plants.medicalSignificance: Infusion of flowers used for headaches, colds; mild antiseptic properties.

plants.name: Banana
plants.origin: Southeast Asia (including India, Malaysia, Indonesia, Philippines)
plants.economicUse: Staple fruit crop; used raw, cooked, fried, dried, or processed into chips, flour, jams, and beverages. Fibres used for textiles and paper.
plants.vedicSignificance: Used in Ayurveda as Kadali or Vazhaipazham. Balances Pitta and Vata. Flower, stem, and root used for treating kidney stones, diabetes, and ulcers.
plants.medicalSignificance: Rich in potassium, magnesium, vitamin B6. Helps digestion, relieves constipation. Soothes ulcers, acidity. Unripe banana helps in diabetes control. Flower used for ulcers and bronchitis.

plants.name: Anjira
plants.origin: Western Asia / Mediterranean region
plants.economicUse: Rich in dietary fiber, potassium, calcium, magnesium, and antioxidants. Traditionally used for: Digestive aid (laxative), Supporting heart health, Managing diabetes and anemia, Soothing respiratory issues and inflammation.
plants.medicalSignificance: Digestive health, anti-inflammatory, anemia relief, mild laxative.

plants.name: Jarige
plants.origin: Western Ghats (India), also found in Southeast Asia
plants.economicUse: It is a sour fruit is dried and powdered to act as a substitute for tamarind in traditional curries and chutneys in Karnataka cuisine. Known for its distinct tangy flavor. The fruit rind is rich in hydroxycitric acid (HCA) and is used in making spice mixes and regional condiments.
plants.vedicSignificance: In folk medicine, the dried fruit is used to improve appetite, relieve digestive discomfort, and support liver function. Acts as a cooling agent and is sometimes included in Ayurvedic or local remedies for weight management, acidity, and mild fever.
plants.medicalSignificance: Garcinia species show antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and hepatoprotective properties. Digestive health, appetite stimulant, liver support, weight control aid.

plants.name: Coconut var. Kesuvari
plants.vernacularName: Coconut var. Kesuvari / Orange / Kutiyadi / Kera Ganga / Gangabondam
plants.origin: Indo-Malaya region (likely coastal Southeast Asia or Pacific Islands)
plants.economicUse: Oil extraction (copra). Tender nut water industry. Coir production (from husk). Timber (from trunk – used in construction and furniture). Used in soaps, cosmetics, and food industries.
plants.vedicSignificance: Mentioned in Ayurveda as Narikela. Found in Charaka Samhita, Sushruta Samhita, and Bhavaprakasha Nighantu. Considered a satvik (pure and life-supporting) food. Used in many Ayurvedic formulations and rituals.
plants.medicalSignificance: Antiviral, antibacterial, and antifungal properties (coconut oil). Hydration and electrolyte balance (tender coconut water). Improves digestion and boosts immunity. Used in Ayurvedic remedies for skin and hair health.

plants.name: Bow fruit
plants.vernacularName: Bow fruit / Bow wood / Cross‑berry / Four Corners / Basbessie
plants.origin: Southern Africa, including parts of South Africa and Zimbabwe, and also found in regions of East Africa and Australia
plants.economicUse: Ornamental planting, wildlife food source, minor fruit crop. Eaten fresh, fermented juice, occasionally cooked in milk or made into jams.

His valor is written as "Raghuvamsha” by Kalidasa. who distributed gold leaves (symbolized by Apta leaves) after his victorious campaign. After ascending the throne, King Raghuraja undertook a Digvijaya Yatra, a traditional military campaign to conquer the four cardinal directions. He defeated many kings and established peace and dharma across Bharat (India). After achieving victory over all directions, he returned to his capital Ayodhya. Upon returning, a young Brahmin  named Kautsa approached King Raghu to seek 14 crores of gold coins to offer to his guru, Sage Varatantu, as Guru Dakshina. King Raghu, despite having just completed the costly campaign and depleted his treasury, promised the full amount. To fulfill his promise, Raghu prayed Kubera, the God of Wealth who then showered gold coins from the heavens near Ayodhya. The gold that rained from the heavens fell upon the Apta trees, and the leaves turned golden as a result. From then, Apta leaves came to be known as “Sona” (gold) and a symbol of prosperity and divine, exchanged during Vijayadashami (Dussehra), the day symbolizing the victory of good over evil.
